#54237. Latest Update: Florida’s invasive pythons don’t always stay on the ground, and about 1 in 7 adult sightings were up in trees

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (896 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Florida’s invasive pythons don’t always stay on the ground, and about 1 in 7 adult sightings were up in trees

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (896 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A USGS study found that invasive Burmese pythons in Florida sometimes climb trees, especially in winter, raising concerns for nesting birds.
  • Burmese pythons invading southern Florida are not primarily tree-dwellers, but some of them climb.
  • According to recent reports, for 168 juveniles, the share was about 17 percent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A USGS study found that invasive Burmese pythons in Florida sometimes climb trees, especially in winter, raising concerns for nesting birds.

Burmese pythons invading southern Florida are not primarily tree-dwellers, but some of them climb. Among 188 radio-tracked adults, about 14 percent, or roughly 1 in 7, were found in a tree or shrub at least once, according to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS).

According to recent reports, for 168 juveniles, the share was about 17 percent. Across more than 4,000 observations, however, fewer than 3 percent placed a python in a tree or shrub.

Both age groups were most likely to climb in December and January, the cooler months of southern Florida’s dry season.

In a recent development, each observation came from locating a snake through radio telemetry, not from a chance sighting. Tracking ran from November 2017 to December 2024 in Major Cypress National Preserve.

Lisa McBride, a biologist at the USGS Fort Collins Science Center, is the study’s first author.

A public USGS data release lists 112 tracking events in trees or shrubs, involving 56 different pythons.

According to recent reports, the first python was observed in the Everglades in 1979, but no more were seen until 1995. The species now breeds in the preserve and is spreading through south Florida.

Sources indicate that burmese pythons, one of Florida’s invasive reptiles, are notoriously difficult to find. By some estimates, the probability of detecting an individual python can be less than 5 percent.

Recent findings suggest that adults in trees were seen basking, resting, brooding eggs or gathering with other pythons. Juveniles rested, basked or moved between tree limbs.

Most adults found in trees during the peak climbing months were basking, a behavior that lets reptiles absorb heat from their surroundings.

The researchers suggest pythons may use trees and shrubs at that time of year to maintain a high body temperature.

Industry observers note that in February 2022, one adult male basked atop a Brazilian peppertree about 16 feet (5 meters) above the ground. It then climbed to the crown of a cabbage palm, about 23 feet (7 meters) up.

A female brooded her eggs in a fallen, hollow cypress tree about 6.5 feet (2 meters) above the ground in May 2022.

A juvenile female rested on a pond apple tree about 5 feet (1.5 meters) up that same May.

A USGS video reveals a juvenile female moving across the branches of a dahoon holly tree in the preserve.

The higher share among juveniles may reflect an ontogenetic shift, a change in habitat use as an animal grows, the researchers suggest.

The probability of finding a python in a tree generally fell as its weight rose. Smaller snakes may move through branches more easily than heavy adults.

Still, trees with strong branches, such as Brazilian peppertrees and live oaks, supported some of the largest pythons tracked.

Sources indicate that adults caught in Florida average 6 to 9 feet (1.8 to 2.7 meters), according to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC). The species can reach 19 feet (5.8 meters), however.

Native from India to lower China, the Malay Peninsula and some islands of the East Indies, Burmese pythons are semi-aquatic and excellent climbers.

The exact route of their introduction is unknown. Pythons likely escaped from a breeding facility destroyed during Hurricane Andrew, and pet pythons have likely been released in and around the Everglades.

Industry observers note that the months when adult pythons were most likely to be in trees overlap with the nesting season of several wading-bird species. Earlier studies documented pythons preying on nests of great egrets and white ibises in the Everglades.

Industry observers note that no python was seen preying on birds in trees during the tracking. The USGS cautioned that the overlap does not mean tree use is causing bird declines.

Rather, it identifies another behavior that could bring an invasive predator into contact with vulnerable animals, and an area for continued research.

More than 25 percent of captured pythons have birds in their stomachs.

Before 2000, mammals were encountered frequently during nocturnal road surveys in Everglades National Park. Road surveys from 2003 to 2011 then recorded a 99.3 percent drop in raccoon observations as pythons spread.

Opossum observations fell by 98.9 percent and bobcat observations by 87.5 percent. The same surveys failed to detect rabbits.

Some reports put the south Florida python population anywhere from 5,000 to 180,000 snakes, though the best estimates so far place it closer to 30,000.

Industry observers note that almost 28,000 wild Burmese pythons have been removed from Florida’s environment and reported to the FWC since 2000. The 2026 Florida Python Challenge alone removed 280, with 907 participants from 30 U.S. states, Canada and Vietnam.

The South Florida Water Management District also pays agents an hourly rate to hunt pythons. They earn $50 for each snake up to 4 feet (1.2 meters), $25 for each additional foot (0.3 meters) and $200 for each verified active nest.

Seasonal data on tree use “could improve the effectiveness of removal efforts by management agencies,” the authors wrote.

Knowing when pythons climb could also help scientists understand how the snakes interact with the Greater Everglades ecosystem.

The study was published in the journal Journal of Herpetology.

#54234. Breaking: This scientist proves which problems computers can’t solve rapidly

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (384 w)

Breaking: This scientist proves which problems computers can’t solve rapidly

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (384 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, dor Minzer remembers sitting in an undergraduate computation class at Tel Aviv University.
  • In a recent development, “My part is actually to prove not only do I not know how to do it, but I can prove that it’s impossible,” Minzer says.
  • Sources indicate that minzer’s hard work has paid off.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, dor Minzer remembers sitting in an undergraduate computation class at Tel Aviv University. He was intrigued by his professor and soon found himself pulled into a latest world: the mystifying intersection of math and computation, first laid out by Alan Turing during World War II. Working with the professor, Minzer became deeply interested in the limitations of what computers can and can’t do.

In a recent development, “My part is actually to prove not only do I not know how to do it, but I can prove that it’s impossible,” Minzer says. “You have to really be curious.”.

Sources indicate that minzer’s hard work has paid off. In 2018, he proved a theoretical computer science problem called the 2-to-2 games conjecture. It asks whether computers can efficiently distinguish games where almost all rules can be satisfied from those where almost none can be satisfied, when the rules have a strict structure.

Industry observers note that in September, Minzer and his two graduate students at MIT posted a 95-page milestone paper on the unique games conjecture, which builds off the 2-to-2 conjecture. The paper wasn’t quite ready, but they published to get ahead of a press release from OpenAI, describing its proof for the same problem, slated for only days later. It’s a situation that many mathematicians have found themselves in this year as AI companies flood the field with findings at lightning speed.

Minzer notes it’s critical to remember that math, and all the research and contemplation behind it, is very human. “It’s a human activity,” he says. “Research is sort of a living organism, a living body.”.

It has been revealed that minzer teaches his own students now. Some days, he talks to his class and gets the sense that nobody is paying attention. But other days, he gets a few students that participate. They have ideas, they’re excited, and they remind him of his own days as a graduate student.

Industry observers note that “I feel like now I feel like I’m passing the torch,” he notes. “Before you have a Ph.D. adviser, you’re like a new person in a dark room. There are infinite places to go. Your Ph.D. adviser is the person that holds your hand and says, ‘Okay, let’s walk here.’”.

A dinosaur found by a Montana rancher on her land in 2019 sold for $47.3 million, over five times its top estimate

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (895 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Nanotyrannus skeleton nicknamed Jodi sold for $47.3 million at Sotheby's in 2026, raising concerns about scientific access to rare fossils.
  • A Nanotyrannus skeleton nicknamed “Jodi” sold at Sotheby’s in Fresh York on October 27, 2026, for a final price of $47.3 million.
  • Jodi Pierson found the skeleton in 2019 on her privately owned land near the town of Jordan, in Garfield County, Montana.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Nanotyrannus skeleton nicknamed Jodi sold for $47.3 million at Sotheby's in 2026, raising concerns about scientific access to rare fossils.

A Nanotyrannus skeleton nicknamed “Jodi” sold at Sotheby’s in Fresh York on October 27, 2026, for a final price of $47.3 million. Its pre-sale estimate was $6 million to $9 million.

Jodi Pierson found the skeleton in 2019 on her privately owned land near the town of Jordan, in Garfield County, Montana.

Six bidders competed for more than 12 minutes, the auction house mentioned. Jodi is now the second most valuable dinosaur ever sold at auction.

The record belongs to “Gus,” a Tyrannosaurus rex skeleton that sold at Sotheby’s New York for $50.1 million on July 14, 2026.

According to recent reports, according to Guinness World Records, Gus broke the record set by “Apex,” a Stegosaurus also sold at Sotheby’s New York. Apex fetched $44.6 million on July 17, 2024.

It has been revealed that sotheby’s reports its results including the buyer’s premium, the fee added to the winning bid. The hammer price for Jodi has not been made public.

Sources indicate that jodi was the only lot in its own dedicated sale. Neither the buyer nor the seller has been named.

Its listed provenance is a private collection that acquired the skeleton in 2021.

Industry observers note that sotheby’s lists Jodi as Nanotyrannus cf. lancensis, from the Hell Creek Formation, about 67 million years old. The abbreviation “cf.” marks a provisional identification.

A crew of seven, including Pierson and Clayton Phipps, dug up the skeleton in a single field season. It comprises about 191 fossil bone elements from one individual.

In a recent development, its virtually complete skull has 53 bones and roughly 50 teeth. The rarely preserved wishbone is intact, and about half of the belly ribs, or gastralia, survived.

In a recent development, missing parts were restored with 3D-printed and sculpted elements, and the mounted skeleton measures about 19.6 feet (6 meters) from nose to tail. It stands about 9 feet 6 inches (2.9 meters) tall, not 6 feet 5 inches (2 meters) as first listed.

Sources indicate that the auction house describes the animal as an adult, based on its overall size and degree of bone development. It cites no peer-reviewed study of the skeleton.

Sources indicate that at the Frieze Masters art fair in 2023, the same skeleton was exhibited as a juvenile T. rex.

Sources indicate that for decades, many paleontologists argued that Nanotyrannus fossils were simply young T. rex. The debate centered on a skull collected in Montana in 1942 by the Cleveland Museum of Natural History.

According to recent reports, in 1988, a team that included museum curator Dr. Michael Williams named it Nanotyrannus lancensis. In December 2025, a study in Science found that the skull’s throat bone had stopped growing, indicating a mature animal.

In October 2025, a study in Nature concluded that the tyrannosaur in the “Dueling Dinosaurs” fossil was a fully grown Nanotyrannus lancensis. Growth rings and fused vertebrae put its age at about 20 years.

In a recent development, that animal had larger forelimbs, more teeth and fewer tail vertebrae than T. rex, the North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences reported.

After examining more than 200 tyrannosaur fossils, the researchers also named a second species, Nanotyrannus lethaeus, after the River Lethe of Greek mythology.

“This fossil doesn’t just settle the debate. It flips decades of T. rex research on its head,” Lindsay Zanno, head of paleontology at the North Carolina museum and a co-author of the study, noted in 2025.

Before the Gus auction, the Society of Vertebrate Paleontology issued a statement on scientifically significant fossils. It called for them to be permanently curated in accredited museums, universities and other public research institutions.

Without provisions for long-term access, private ownership may permanently diminish opportunities for future research, education and public engagement, the society warned. It also recognized the key role of private landowners, amateur fossil enthusiasts and commercial excavators.

“The discovery of an crucial fossil is only the beginning of its scientific story,” stated Kristina Curry Rogers, the society’s vice president at the time.

Industry observers note that “Many of the most significant advances in paleontology have come years or even decades after a fossil was collected,” she noted. Newly introduced analytical methods and technologies allowed scientists to ask entirely new questions of specimens already housed in museums.

Industry observers note that after the Jodi sale, Curry Rogers and Zanno published an opinion piece on fossil auctions. They wrote that they hope the upcoming owner will make Jodi available for scientific study and public education.

Under Montana law, fossils are part of the surface estate, so they normally belong to whoever owns the land.

Sources indicate that the provision, enacted in 2019, claims the word “minerals” does not include fossils unless a deed or other instrument clearly states otherwise. A landowner can sever fossil rights from the land through a clear and express grant.

Sotheby’s offered Jodi with full rights and documentation certifying its condition, authenticity and the legality of its ownership.

The federal Paleontological Resources Preservation Act of 2009 does not apply to state, private or Indian lands, according to the Bureau of Land Management.

The information was obtained from Sotheby’s.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that if you’ve got a viewing site with a clear eastern horizon, this morning offers a great opportunity to spot the solar system’s innermost planet.
  • Located in Libra, the tiny world sits to the far lower left of bright Venus, higher in the sky.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 20: The Moon passes Saturn and Neptune.

Industry observers note that if you’ve got a viewing site with a clear eastern horizon, this morning offers a great opportunity to spot the solar system’s innermost planet. Look for Mercury about an hour before sunrise, when it reaches 7° high and shines at magnitude –0.5. The planet reached its greatest western elongation from our Sun yesterday evening, and is now 20° west of our star in the sky.

Located in Libra, the tiny world sits to the far lower left of bright Venus, higher in the sky. Venus is in the constellation Virgo, standing just north (to the upper left) of the bright star Spica. Another bright star, Arcturus in Boötes, hangs to that pair’s far upper left.

Pull out a telescope to check out the size and phase of each planet. Start with Venus, whose disk spans a hefty 46” — right now larger than Jupiter’s apparent size in our sky. Despite its impressive width, however, the disk of Venus appears as just a sliver, only 19% lit. Slide down to Mercury for comparison, and see that its phase is much larger — 62% — while the planet’s overall apparent width is much smaller, just 7”.

If you’re able, keep watching Mercury day by day in the morning sky. Its gibbous phase will continue growing, reaching 84% lit by the end of the month.

According to recent reports, sunrise: 6:52 A.M.Sunset: 4:39 P.M.Moonrise: 2:29 P.M.Moonset: 3:22 A.M.Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (92%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.

The 8 Best Solar Generators Provide Reliable Backup Power in a Pinch

📅 13 Aug 2021 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3481 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • In a recent development, power stations (i.e., solar generators) have become increasingly popular because they are easy to run, cost less over time than gas generators, and offer eco-friendly, emission-free operation, especially when paired with a solar panel.
  • It has been revealed that unlike fuel-based generators, solar generators can’t create electricity in real time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

In a recent development, power stations (i.e., solar generators) have become increasingly popular because they are easy to run, cost less over time than gas generators, and offer eco-friendly, emission-free operation, especially when paired with a solar panel. Some are small and compact, ideal for off-grid adventures, while larger ones are able to back up critical home circuits during a blackout.

It has been revealed that unlike fuel-based generators, solar generators can’t create electricity in real time. They’re giant battery packs, not true generators, and need to be recharged using alternating current (AC) power or solar panels, the latter of which often takes many hours in ideally sunny conditions.

Industry observers note that despite those distinctions compared to portable generators, there’s nothing more convenient than a power station for charging or running everything you need for day-to-day life—phones and laptops, lights, and even a small appliance or two. Plus, it’s nice to have a device that doesn’t produce carbon emissions and replenishes itself freely from the sun’s rays. Whether you’re seeking a highly portable option or need one that’s heavy-duty enough for extended use, these are the best solar generators we’ve tested and researched to date.

Industry observers note that to pick the best solar generators, we tested some of these power stations for charging capacity, ease of use, weight, and different use cases. Our picks were reviewed by Popular Mechanics editor Brad Ford, who provided input for the larger-capacity units. Other models on this list were reviewed by test editor David Dritsas or freelance writer Maggie Slepian.

In a recent development, our primary concerns were portability and convenience. Ease of use was also important—was the display easy to read? Did the screen readouts make sense? Bonus points if we could tell how much power is available at a glance. In the past few years, these criteria have become easier to meet. There are now plenty of compact, affordable units that have better charging capabilities than before.

Very few power stations of this size can handle as much solar input power as the Bluetti Apex 200. With two input types—low-voltage XT60 (up to 1,000 watts) and high-voltage MC4 (up to 2,000 watts)—it can accept up to 3,000 watts of solar power. If you had the panels and ideal weather, you could fully charge this station in less than 2 hours—even faster than plugging it into the wall. That’s impressive.

It also balances nicely between being a portable station and a home backup solution. It offers 3,200 watts of continuous power (it says 3,600 on the front, but that’s only if it’s connected to an expansion battery). We were able to power a refrigerator for a full 27 hours on a single charge, and estimated the battery efficiency at 90 percent, which is very good. Meanwhile, the 2,560-watt-hour battery capacity is expandable by adding up to six additional batteries. Using Bluetti’s largest battery, the B500K, you could build a massive 33-kilowatt-hour system.

While 3,600 watts isn’t enough to power a whole home, you could power a couple of circuits through a manual transfer switch using the 120-volt 30-amp output. But keep in mind that there’s no 240-volt support, so you can’t use it to power high-voltage appliances like electric dryers.

Sources indicate that as a portable station, the Apex 200 has a lot to offer. At 59 pounds, it’s not too hard to move around the house or in and out of a vehicle. And there are several great DC power options, including a bank of USB outlets (two are high-power USB-C) and both 10- and 30-amp, 12-volt outputs. We also love that the AC ports can individually be turned on and off using the mobile app; this helps improve overall runtime.

Since very few stations can match its max solar input capacity, we concluded that the Apex 200 is definitely a top choice for anyone who wants a power station that can recharge using the sun’s rays, but also offers the versatility of being used on the road or at home.

Full Bluetti Apex 200 Power Station Review.

This model replaces the original Jackery 1000, but many of the same observations made of the first model still apply. The new version has a slightly higher capacity of 1,070 watt-hours and uses a newer lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) battery, which is a newer battery technology that offers a longer lifespan (4,000 cycles versus 500 cycles for this model) and better performance in extreme temperatures.

In a recent development, expert Maggie Slepian used the previous model on a media trip where she had to keep multiple camera batteries charged during a weeklong outing. She found that while the capacity was lower than you'll find with others on this list, it actually powers items for longer than some higher-capacity models. She also charged her photographer’s camera batteries while charging the power bank on solar power (it was a very sunny winter day), which proved effective and efficient.

The newer V2 model has seven ports, including three AC outlets, two USB-C ports (one 30-watt and one 100-watt), a 12-volt car port, and one standard 18-watt USB-A outlet. It charges a typical laptop eight times or powers a small refrigerator or an electric cooler for over 15 hours.

The Jackery Explorer 1000 V2 charges with a 200-watt solar panel or a 12-volt outlet in your vehicle while you’re on the move. It has fairly standard charging times, with 11.5 hours in a car outlet, 6.5 hours for solar panels, and just 5.5 hours to fully charge in a wall outlet. This won’t be your best bet for powering larger appliances, but it’s an ideal power station for smaller items and off-grid camping.

Industry observers note that the EcoFlow Delta Pro is a large portable power station with an output that rivals some gas portable generators. When sold in a bundle with solar panels, like the package with two 220-watt portable panels we tested, it becomes a powerful solar generator. With an output of 3,600 watts, the Delta Pro can charge multiple appliances, and the output has the ability to bump up to 4,500 watts with its built-in X-Boost technology if more power is needed.

According to recent reports, to get an idea of the run time, we used the Delta Pro to power a full-size, 25-cubic-foot refrigerator—which it did for a remarkable 51 hours and 24 minutes. When recharged from a standard outlet, it took only two hours and 36 minutes. But it also charges with the included adapter, at electric vehicle charging stations, with a DC car adapter, or with the solar panels that come with the unit. Through the 30-amp connection, you can also connect this to a transfer switch to directly power select circuits in your home.

In a recent development, like any power station with a large battery capacity, it will take a long time, perhaps nearly two days, to recharge this station using the bundled 220-watt solar panels. The good news is the Delta Pro accepts up to 1,600 watts of solar input, so it can charge faster by connecting more panels.

The heavy-duty wheels and telescoping handle on Anker’s Solix F3000 are easy to use, allow you to stand upright when pulling, and are a dream for people who regularly find themselves moving their power station around, whether it’s at a campsite or to different parts of the house during a power outage.

Along with convenience, this generator is a powerhouse with the capacity to easily run your refrigerator or a greenhouse heater, or keep your RV bright and warm.

According to recent reports, we were impressed with Anker’s app, which allows us to check the charging status or power being generated without continually going outside to check. The app also lets you turn the power to the AC and USB ports on and off remotely, keeping tabs on how much energy is being utilized.

It has been revealed that the Solix F3000 has 11 ports, including two car ports, an RV-specific outlet, four AC ports, three USB-C charging ports, and two USB-A. In sunny conditions and moderate temperatures, it recharges with a 400-watt solar panel in just a few hours and supports up to 2,400 watts of solar input.

In a recent development, one of Jackery’s most recent solar generators is also its most rugged, able to withstand the elements better than most. It achieves this with an IP65 weatherproof rating, molded rubber port covers, a shockproof enclosure, and a bottom drainage system, which is part of a titanium alloy cooling structure that helps keep water out of the enclosure.

Sources indicate that we got a chance to see these features up close and were impressed by them all, as well as a very sturdy enclosure that, thanks to the cooling system design, eliminates any side vents that could allow water to get inside. It feels strong; you could bang this station around without worrying too much about damaging it. The only downside is that this denser construction adds a bit of weight.

As a power station, it delivers 1,800 watts of output with a battery capacity of 1,536 watt-hours. That’s enough power for a weekend camping trip or for running low-powered small appliances and some lighting during an emergency. As a solar generator, it can handle up to 800 watts of input from a portable panel. We paired it with a Jackery 200-watt panel, and it worked well. Overall, if your off-road adventures often get a little dirty, but you need some extra power, the Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra Power Station is a good one to have at your side.

Full Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra Power Station Review.

Recent findings suggest that the latest version of the Goal Zero Yeti 1500 is a well-designed power station that’s ideal for off-grid camping situations where dust, wind, and potentially wet conditions are always on the table. This 2,000-watt power station is weatherproof with an IPX4 rating and features outlet shields that cover the ports and inputs. Each section is well-lit by an LED light that’s individually turned on or off using a manual button or the mobile app (and will shut off if not used after a certain period).

Sources indicate that there’s a healthy number of outputs on the Yeti 1500, including four 120-volt AC outlets, four (two are high-powered) USB-A ports, and four 12-volt connections. We simulated an emergency blackout and managed to run a cable modem with a WiFi router, a lamp, a TV, and a tower fan, while charging a phone and a laptop through the USB-C ports. Given the station’s output and capacity, there was enough power for over two days of use (conveniently shown on the main display), and there was plenty of room to spare for a few more devices.

To test its solar capabilities, we paired the Yeti 1500 with a Nomad 200-watt portable solar panel and connected it using the high-voltage DC input, which accepts up to 600 watts; however, it also features a low-voltage input that accepts up to 300 watts for smaller panel arrays. Because both inputs can be used simultaneously, you could theoretically pair with two arrays for up to 900 watts, which is a high amount of input for a station of this size.

Of course, no portable panel operates at 100 percent efficiency. Even on a sunny, cloudless day with no shade-causing obstructions, the input readings indicated anywhere from 125 to 145 watts. After initiating a recharge with only 5 percent capacity left, it would take at least 10.5 hours in those conditions to recharge. That’s actually not bad. An average of about 70 percent efficiency for a portable panel is good.

Full Goal Zero Yeti 1500 Review.

This power station takes solar recharging seriously. The Elite 300 can accept up to 1,200 watts of input, which is a high amount for a station this size. We paired it with a 250-watt portable panel and, on a fully sunny day, got around 260 watts of input. That’s the typical efficiency of a portable panel (again, you’ll never get 100 percent). But pair it with some larger panels, and you’ll get even more.

It has been revealed that it also boasts an impressive battery capacity of just over 3,000 watt-hours and 2,400 watts of output, which is high for a station of this size. Plus, it includes a 120-volt 30-amp port, which is handy for connecting it to a small RV or pop-up camper, allowing you to run small appliances and water pumps. It’s not enough power to run a heating or cooling system for a significant amount of time, but for lights, small appliances, and other items that need power, this station will deliver.

According to recent reports, if there’s one downside we found, it’s that there’s no way to add an expansion battery to increase your capacity. That’s not a huge detractor, but it’s something we’ve seen in stations even smaller than this one. But at the end of the day, the Bluetti Elite 300 solar generator offers the right balance between a midsize power station that delivers a lot of power and run time, and a station that is compact and portable enough to be perfectly suited for an outdoor adventure.

Full Bluetti Elite 300 Solar Generator Review.

It has been revealed that the Anker Solix C2000 power station can deliver the full 2,400 watts of output to the bank of five AC outlets—something similar stations don’t offer. This allows you to power several things at once, like a refrigerator, toaster, router, and chargers, all at the same time.

During our tests, we were able to take full advantage of this, powering a refrigerator (by itself for up to 18 hours), along with some high-powered appliances, like a four-slot toaster and an electric kettle (though not the last two at the same time).

Industry observers note that another interesting ability of the C2000 is that you can fast charge it from AC power up to 1,800 watts, but that recharging rate remains consistent if you’re powering other devices at the same time (we confirmed this with a wattmeter). For example, we ran a 1,400-watt space heater while still recharging at the full 1,800-watt rate. Other power stations offer similar fast charging but will throttle the amount of power coming into the station while powering devices.

Sources indicate that for solar recharging, we were a bit disappointed that this station can only accept 800 watts of input; other stations of this size accept more. But when solar was plugged in, it worked well. We connected it to a 200-watt Anker portable panel, and in full sun, we were getting around 125 to 145 watts of input, which is pretty good as these types of panels go. The C2000 is not IPX-rated for any type of weather resistance, however, so we would not recommend leaving this station sitting outside if the weather turns wet.

Full Anker Solix C2000 Power Station Review.

Power stations use watts and watt-hours to express size and capacity. Watts (size) refer to how much power it produces. For example, if you need to run a 900-watt microwave, you’ll need a station that outputs at least that much power (ideally more, since factory specs are never exact).

Industry observers note that meanwhile, watt-hours (capacity) give you an idea of how long devices can be powered continuously, though how much time depends on the amount of power being drawn—watt-hours don’t dictate a set time frame. Higher-powered devices will drain the battery a lot faster than lower-powered ones.

That may seem confusing, but a simple equation gives you an approximate idea of how it works: total watt-hours (of the generator) ÷ watts (of the device) = hours the power station runs.

For example, if you had a power station with a 2,048-watt-hour capacity and wanted to run a 750-watt space heater consistently at its highest setting, it would probably run for around 2.5 hours, so long as nothing else is plugged in. But for a refrigerator, whose power draw fluctuates between 10 and 300 watts (depending on how often the compressor turns on), you might be able to run it for nearly 24 hours.

Keep in mind that manufacturer specs are taken from perfect conditions; in the real world, you’ll likely see slightly less capacity from your power station. If you’re not sure how much power the different devices in your home draw, sometimes it’s written on a label, or you can use a device like a wattmeter.

Just as a power station has specifications on output size and capacity, solar panels are rated by how many watts they produce for a device after they convert the sun’s rays into electrical current (e.g., 100 watts, 200 watts, etc.). Because real-world conditions are never perfect, it’s not uncommon for panels to only output 50 to 75 percent (or even lower) of their total potential.

Sources indicate that your panels must also be within the acceptable input range of the power station. For example, connecting a 400-watt solar-panel array to a power station that only accepts 110 watts of solar input can cause an overload and damage the station.

While weight and size don’t directly correlate to the technicalities of power banks, they impact the convenience of each model. Many camping and overlanding setups have limited space, so the more compact models likely have a higher appeal as a result.

Recent findings suggest that that mentioned, most units weigh at least 10 pounds, and the weight and size increase quickly with greater capacities. Before purchasing, consider where you proposal to store the power bank and the space in your vehicle or camper where it will live while you’re on the road. If you plan to use this power bank solely as a home backup option, portability will matter less, but consider how much effort it will take to move it around within your home or in your outdoor space.

Sources indicate that I am a low-maintenance camper, and most of my background is in lightweight backcountry travel. That means I prioritize space-saving and ease-of-use, so my go-to power banks have between 250 and 600 watt-hours, and weigh less than 15 pounds.

This is perfect for a weekend trip, with the on-the-go (car or solar) charging capabilities to put my mind at ease for longer trips. Mostly, I’m charging small items, so one charge lasts a long time. However, plenty of people in the van-life and remote-work world are powering their RVs and vans, and relying on multiple laptop charges. For that, I’d recommend one of the larger units.

Recent findings suggest that A solar-powered generator charges and runs almost anything that requires power—it just depends on the capacity. These generators can charge power tools in the shop, laptops for remote work, and personal devices like Bluetooth headphones and speakers.

A solar-powered generator with a higher power capacity can even power household appliances in the event of a power outage. And the fact that these are solar-compatible means you aren’t reliant on the electrical grid to recharge them.

Every unit on our list has multiple charging options, including wall (AC outlet), car (12-volt), and solar. Each input method charges your unit at a different speed, and solar also depends on the conditions. AC power is the fastest, followed by 12-volt, and then by solar (though a larger solar array could potentially be faster than 12-volt).

I try to charge up my power banks whenever I can, so I’m never caught off guard trying to leave on a trip with a dying power bank. If this happens (which it has), I’ll charge it in my vehicle’s 12-volt port while I’m driving, though this is often slower than solar or a wall unit.

Recent findings suggest that solar power is the most sustainable and typically fastest way to power these—just be sure you have enough wattage in the solar panels to make it effective. I recommend keeping the generator stored with at least an 80 percent charge, and unplugging it once it’s fully charged—keeping it plugged in longer than necessary degrades the battery.

Most units will have a simple readout display showing the remaining battery charge, and it’s a good practice not to allow your battery pack to get below 20 percent.

  • Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

In a recent development, born in Venice, Italy, in 1905, Bruno Rossi attended the University of Bologna, graduating with a doctorate in physics in 1927. When race-based laws inspired by his country’s growing closeness with Nazi Germany meant the Jewish Rossi had to leave Italy, he made his way to the U.S. In 1940, Rossi became an associate professor of physics at Cornell University, and from 1943-1946, he worked on the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos Laboratory. After the war, Rossi joined the faculty of MIT, where he remained until his retirement in the early ’70s.

In a recent development, throughout his long career across countries and institutions, Rossi laid the groundwork for the study of several key fields in astronomy and astrophysics. His research into cosmic rays became the basis of high-energy particle physics, while his pioneering search for cosmic X-rays jump-started X-ray astronomy. Rossi also conducted trailblazing research into the interplanetary medium, and contributed to the development of public policy for space exploration. Rossi passed away at age 88 on Nov. 21, 1993. Today, among other honors and memorials that Rossi accrued, the Bruno B. Rossi Prize for astrophysics is awarded yearly.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

Sources indicate that former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., is seen in a vineyard near his cottage in Civrac-en-Médoc, France, on March 20, 2024. (Ariel Cohen/CQ Roll Call).

In a recent development, former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., a fierce advocate for universal health care and outspoken war critic who served 28 years in Congress, died Thursday at the age of 89, his family confirmed.

In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.

As the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Health Subcommittee, McDermott defended the 2010 Affordable Care Act that expanded health insurance to millions of Americans, while critics complained it did little to control costs.

Sources indicate that “Jim was one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress,” Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., wrote on X. “He was passionate and fearless — and left a tremendous legacy on WA state and its people. My thoughts are with Congressman McDermott’s family and loved ones during this difficult time.”.

When McDermott announced his retirement from Congress in 2016, then-President Barack Obama praised him in a statement as “a much-needed voice for his most vulnerable constituents.”.

Recent findings suggest that born and raised in Illinois, McDermott came from a poor, conservative and deeply religious family. His father, a bond underwriter, and his mother, a telephone operator and homemaker, started a church in the garage of their two-bedroom home. His three siblings slept in one bedroom; his parents in the other. McDermott, the oldest child, had the couch.

He attended the conservative evangelical Wheaton College. His bend toward liberalism began during medical school at the University of Illinois, when he voted for John F. Kennedy in the 1960 presidential election. After a stint in the U.S. Navy Medical Corps from 1968-1970, McDermott won his first seat in the Washington state House in 1970 running on an anti-war platform.

He continued his anti-war stances in Congress, voting against the 2002 resolution authorizing the use of military force in Iraq. In 2013, he opposed U.S. intervention in Syria and was one of only 20 House members to vote against new sanctions on Iran.

Shortly after he retired from Congress, McDermott settled on a fresh life for himself by moving to a small town in southwestern France, where he admired some of the public policies he had fought hard to deliver in Washington with mixed success.

Industry observers note that “I spent 16 years in the Washington state legislature trying to get single-payer health care,” he recalled in a 2024 interview with CQ Roll Call at his home about 90 minutes outside of Bourdeaux. “Then I spent nearly 30 years in Congress trying to get single-payer. Then I came to France and in three months I had single-payer. Was that mind-blowing? You bet.”.

It has been revealed that as he remarked, McDermott dedicated much time in the Washington state legislature to trying to create a single-payer system. When that didn’t work out, he developed the Washington State Basic Health Program, a health coverage system for the unemployed and working poor — the first state program of its kind.

In a recent development, then, once he got to Washington, he tried to work with then-First Lady Hillary Clinton to hatch a federal single-payer program, but that effort came to naught. He later backed the Affordable Care Act and tried to pass his own legislation in 2015 for comprehensive health care coverage.

“The only way to truly ensure that access to quality health care is a right enjoyed by every American is through a single-payer system,” he said in a statement at the time.

McDermott will also be remembered for some of the attacks he leveled against Republicans. In the most notorious incident, he was ordered to pay then-Rep. John A. Boehner of Ohio — who later became speaker — nearly $1.1 million in 2008 after releasing a recording of a 1996 cell phone call between Boehner and then-Speaker Newt Gingrich. McDermott maintained it was worth the fight, and the cost of the settlement, to protect free speech.

Sources indicate that “Jim McDermott was as major as it gets in Washington state politics,” Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., wrote on Facebook. “Smart, funny, and Irish, Jim McDermott will be missed.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, to piece together a fuller picture of what’s out there (alien megastructures around nearby stars, perhaps?), Angelo and her colleagues at the SETI Institute in Mountain View, Calif., are turning to machine learning models.
  • Most of the space weirdos will probably turn out to be total normies — a comet, a newborn star or a star surrounded by lots of gas and dust.

Isabel Angelo spends her days searching the cosmos for exoplanets and signs of extraterrestrial intelligence. But Angelo’s head isn’t in the stars. It’s buried under mountains of 0s and 1s — data from space telescopes old and latest.

In a recent development, to piece together a fuller picture of what’s out there (alien megastructures around nearby stars, perhaps?), Angelo and her colleagues at the SETI Institute in Mountain View, Calif., are turning to machine learning models. These tools are analyzing the troves of telescope data for anomalies — things that look “weird” in space that we don’t know how to explain yet.

Most of the space weirdos will probably turn out to be total normies — a comet, a newborn star or a star surrounded by lots of gas and dust. “These are things that I would expect [the models] to find,” Angelo indicates. “But the goal is to find something that’s not even in any of these categories.”.

Industry observers note that in the meantime, Angelo keeps her whimsy and wonder for space alive by remembering historic moments, like the reveal of the first portrait of a black hole in 2019. The scientists “put all of these telescopes all over the Earth. They wait for the Earth to rotate. They do all this math to construct this one image,” Angelo indicates. “I can’t believe how creative and innovative we have to be to learn about space. It’s such a specific and really fun challenge.”.

The 8 Best Portable Power Stations for Outages and Outings

📅 12 Jun 2020 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4215 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Portable power stations are handy for backup power during outages, off-grid electricity for an RV, or simply charging your laptop and phone while working remotely.
  • In a recent development, portable power stations come in a broad range of sizes from brands like Jackery and EcoFlow, including smaller models capable of charging a few devices and high-capacity backup units to keep your lighting and critical appliances on during a days-long blackout.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Portable power stations are handy for backup power during outages, off-grid electricity for an RV, or simply charging your laptop and phone while working remotely. They’re effectively large bundles of rechargeable lithium-ion batteries, which provide a quiet, exhaust-free alternative to noisy gas-powered portable generators.

In a recent development, portable power stations come in a broad range of sizes from brands like Jackery and EcoFlow, including smaller models capable of charging a few devices and high-capacity backup units to keep your lighting and critical appliances on during a days-long blackout. Plus, most can be recharged using solar panels.

We evaluated eight power stations of varying sizes, focusing on each model’s maximum output, capacity, charging time, and portability. To test max output, we connected enough electronics and appliances to each power station to meet or slightly exceed its listed max output to see how well it could operate at maximum load. We then tested capacity, using an electricity usage monitor to record the total watt-hours each power station produced while running them under a consistent load.

Once they were drained, we charged each power station from 0 to 100 percent using its AC adapter, timing how long it took to get to 80 and 100 percent capacity. Finally, we evaluated each power station’s portability by attempting to carry it or roll it. Other factors that weighed into our decisions included the number and power output of each power station’s inputs and its charging options.

Our test team for this article includes David Dritsas, an editor who covers generators, lawn and garden, and more; Bradley Ford, an editor with more than five years of experience testing and writing about generators, generator maintenance, power tools, and lawn and garden equipment; and Tony Carrick, a frequent Popular Mechanics contributor who covers landscaping, home improvement, gardening, and home security.

Bluetti manages to pack a lot of power into the Elite 200 V2. It has a max output of 2,600 watts (with 3,900-watt startup power) and a 2,073.6-watt-hour capacity, all while being relatively compact.

Industry observers note that we hooked up a miter saw, blender, and space heater, all three of which it powered simultaneously. It easily handled the spike to 4,000 watts to start up the saw, above its listed 3,900-watt starting power, before maintaining an even flow of around 2,500 watts.

The Elite 200 V2 also impressed with the quality of its battery. We recorded 92 percent of its listed 2,073.6-watt-hour capacity, well over the 85 percent average for most portable power stations. It has a quick recharge time for its capacity, going from 0 to 80 percent in 81 minutes and to full in just 107 minutes. And because it uses a LiFePO4 battery, it discharges and recharges for 6,000 cycles before it drops below 80 percent capacity.

The Elite 200 V2 gives you plenty of output and input options for its size, too. Four AC outlets allow you to load up multiple appliances. There are four USB ports for charging smaller devices, a car accessory outlet, and a DC output. Along with its power cord, there’s a port for charging from a car accessory port or with up to 1,000 watts of solar panels.

With a great power-to-weight ratio, the latest version of the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 is a great portable power station for powering a camper or providing backup power for the essentials.

A new and improved version of Jackery’s extremely popular Explorer 1000, the Explorer 1000 V2 features a slightly larger storage capacity, up 70 watt-hours, and a much higher 1,500-watt output—a 50 percent jump from 1,000 watts of the original. This allows you to power devices with higher loads, like an electric grill or a large microwave. Jackery managed this while maintaining the Explorer 1000’s compact size and weight, so it’s still easy to carry with you on a camping trip.

The Explorer 1000 V2 features three standard 120-volt AC outlets, two USB-C ports (30- and 100-watt), one USB-A port (18-watt), and one 12-volt DC outlet. Paired with Jackery’s app, you can monitor the power station locally via Bluetooth or from anywhere when it’s connected via WiFi. The app allows for checking charge levels and estimated run time, as well as toggling any of the outputs on or off. Plugged into the wall, the power station charges in under two hours. It’s also possible to charge it from your vehicle in up to 12 hours.

In a recent development, performance-wise, the 1000 V2 did well powering a 25-cubic-foot refrigerator for 18 hours and 22 minutes, which is better performance than we’ve gotten from other tested 1000-watt models. Under a constant load of 475 watts (that’s a little less than a small coffee maker), it ran for 1 hour and 57 minutes.

This power station offers a lot of bang for the buck. Sure, it isn’t going to power your house through a days-long outage, but it offers a lot of nice features for the price, making it one of the better values out there, especially if you pick it up on sale.

What is most impressive about the Anker S2000 power station is its ability to maximize its runtime. During our testing, we were able to run a full-sized refrigerator for just over 24 hours, which is nearly six hours longer than other power stations we’ve tested with comparable capacity.

It does this using a technology that recognizes the type of device plugged in and adjusts the inverter's frequency to match the type of demand. This, in theory, helps reduce the amount of wasted power. From what we can tell, it works very well.

Sources indicate that the S2000 is fairly well equipped, too, with five outlets for AC power (two are in the back) and a bank of USB ports for home use, and can operate as an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) for 10-millisecond automated backup. With only 1,500 watts of output, it may struggle with some high-power appliances like a large microwave, but for many people, this station can deliver power during a blackout and keep you up and running for a long time.

Industry observers note that one of the standout features of Bluetti’s Apex 200 is a maximum solar input of up to 3,000 watts. You rarely find that much input power for a station of this size. There are two sets of DC inputs for this: low-voltage XT60 input (up to 1,000 watts) and high-voltage MC4 input (up to 2,000 watts). If you have the panels and enough perfect direct sunlight to achieve this full potential, you could fully charge this station in less than two hours using the sun’s rays.

Beyond that, the Apex 200 is a fairly robust power station, with 3,200 watts of continuous power. (It claims 3,600 on the front, but that’s only if it’s connected to an expansion battery.) I ran my refrigerator for a full 27 hours on a single charge, and when I tested it for battery efficiency, I estimated it at about 90 percent, which is very good for a power station. There’s also a 120-volt 30-amp output if you wanted to run a few circuits in your home by hooking up to a manual transfer switch. Just keep in mind that there’s no 240-volt support, so you can’t use it to power high-voltage appliances like electric dryers.

Industry observers note that the 2,560-watt-hour battery capacity isn't huge—at least not for home backup—but you can expand it by adding up to six additional batteries. That could add up to over 33 kilowatt-hours if you use the largest batteries Bluetti offers, the B500K. That’s massive.

Even with all this power, the Apex 200 is still a fairly portable station. Weighing 59 pounds, it’s not too hard to move around the house or in and out of a vehicle. So, when you’re not using it for home backup, it’s perfect for taking on a long outdoor trip or for powering an RV when a site hookup is not available.

Full Bluetti Apex 200 Power Station Review.

Recent findings suggest that this is one of the most rugged power stations we’ve seen yet. The Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra features an IP65 weatherproof rating, molded rubber port covers, a shockproof enclosure, and a bottom drainage system and cooling structure that help keep water out of the enclosure. All work together to resist the elements better than most power stations can.

Sources indicate that the unique cooling system was particularly interesting. A titanium alloy plate within the structure helps dissipate heat without the need for multiple fans and eliminates the need for any side vents (typical in most power stations) that could allow droplets of water in. Meanwhile, you can remove an external plate on the bottom and dry it if water does make its way in.

The 1,800 watts of output power and 1,536 watt-hours of battery capacity are decent if you’re taking this camping for the weekend and need to recharge devices, run a low-powered small appliance or two, and plug in some lighting. But don’t expect to run something like a space heater for very long, though.

Full Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra Power Station Review.

Industry observers note that the S5000 is the second power station in Anker's S-series, which features inverter efficiency technology that helps to reduce wasted energy when the inverter is idling or running lower-powered devices. We were impressed with how this technology performed in the S2000, and this model matched that performance.

Industry observers note that we ran this through several tests, and the battery efficiency proved to be around 97 percent (the industry average is around 89 percent). For example, we left the AC inverter idling for 18 hours, and the battery remained at 100 percent capacity. Meanwhile, another station we idled at the same time lost 19 percent of its available power. That was impressive.

Sources indicate that the next most impressive attribute about the S5000 is its size. It’s at least half the size of other power stations that feature 5,000 watt-hours of capacity and includes just as many outputs, including a 240-volt, 30-amp outlet. It also has both high- and low-powered DC inputs that enable up to 3,000 watts of solar power input if you have the panels to generate that. You can also recharge at up to 4,500 watts using a direct DC connection to Anker's 5500 Smart Tri-Fuel generator.

With only 4,500 watts of total output, we wouldn’t call this a contender for true whole-home backup (Anker’s E-10 system is a better option for that), but the S5000 can deliver a decent amount to power an RV, run lights and appliances during an emergency, or even a couple of critical circuits.

It has been revealed that during our hands-on test, Goal Zero’s newest Yeti 1500 impressed us with its capable performance and sturdy construction. It’s the replacement for an older model and improves on its predecessor with improved weatherproofing, more outputs, and a better battery.

In a recent development, this 2,000-watt power station is clearly designed for outdoor use with an IPX4 water-resistance rating and latest outlet shields that cover the ports and inputs when you’re not using them. That’s great for dusty conditions. Each section is nicely illuminated by an LED light and can be individually turned on/off using a manual button or the mobile app (and will shut off if not used after a duration of time). These additions make it perfect for camping or other outdoor uses. You can’t leave it out in the rain, but getting a bit of water on it won’t be a concern.

We loved the increased number of outputs on the Yeti 1500. There are now four 120-volt AC outlets and six USB ports: four USB-C (two are high-powered) and two USB-A ports, plus four 12-volt connections (though two of those are proprietary for Goal Zero accessories and not all that useful in our estimation). There are also inputs for AC power, 12-volt DC, and inputs for both low- and high-voltage solar power that can be used simultaneously. Theoretically, you could recharge this station with up to 900 watts of eco-friendly electrical current.

Sources indicate that as part of our test, we simulated a blackout at home and managed to run a cable modem/Wi-Fi router, a lamp, a TV, and a tower fan, while simultaneously charging a phone and a laptop through the USB-C ports. Given the station’s output and capacity, there was enough power for over two days of use (conveniently shown on the main display), and there was plenty of room to spare for a few more devices.

In a recent development, the mobile app was easy to use and chock-full of great information on energy consumption. The only problem we had was maintaining a stable Bluetooth connection. It needed to be manually paired every time we went to use it, which was annoying. Wi-Fi is available, but that’s not so useful when you are off-grid.

We should warn you that the Yeti 1500 is heavy at 53 pounds. If you’re taking it on a trip, you’ll need a bit of strength to lug it around. That aside, the 2026 Yeti 1500 is a well-designed power station that’s ideal for off-grid camping, especially when there are dusty or wet conditions. We’d happily take it on our next camping trip.

Full Goal Zero Yeti 1500 Review.

Though it’s no longer EcoFlow’s flagship backup power solution, the original Delta Pro is still a massive power station with a good amount of electrical output. The brand claims it powers nearly any appliance, and after testing, we’re inclined to agree. With an output of 3,600 watts, it can handle multiple appliances, and it’s possible to bump the output to 4,500 watts with its built-in X-Boost technology if you need more power.

In a recent development, in testing, we ran it with a continuous 470-watt load for 6 hours and 57 minutes, as indicated on the Delta Pro’s display. Of course, in a home backup during a power outage situation, we would run only the bare essentials to conserve power. To that end, we used it to power a full-size, 25-cubic-foot refrigerator, which it did for a remarkable 51 hours and 24 minutes.

Recharging the power station from empty using a standard 120-volt home outlet, it recharged to full capacity in 2 hours and 36 minutes. There’s also an included adapter for charging the system at EV charging stations, with solar panels (sold separately), with a car charger, or combinations of these to speed things up.

The Delta Pro’s display screen provides all the key information you need to manage your power consumption. We frequently checked the screen during testing to see the unit’s charge level, current load, and estimated run time at the current discharge rate.

Sources indicate that all of this information is accessible through EcoFlow’s app, which was the most intuitive and easiest to use of those tested. We connected the app both locally using Bluetooth and remotely via WiFi to monitor the power station from anywhere. We could also toggle outlets on and off remotely, which is helpful if you’re trying to manage power station output to extend the battery life.

We’ve tested the brand’s Whole-Home Backup Kit, which includes two of the power stations and a dual-voltage hub used to connect to your home service panel via a transfer switch. We used this setup to power critical circuits in a Northeast Pennsylvania home in late winter.

The Delta Pro Whole Home Kit ran just over 24 hours, powering kitchen outlets, a full-size refrigerator, a chest freezer, a cable modem and wireless network, and a hot water boiler. Plus, having charged these two Delta Pro power stations previously, we found that they were able to hold a full charge for a full eight months.

Testing was performed under normal usage conditions—run time could easily be extended by employing standard power-conservation strategies like lowering the thermostat, powering the fridge and freezer for four hours on and four hours off, and only opening them when absolutely necessary.

EcoFlow’s Delta Pro Whole Home Kit is a legitimate home backup system that can operate inside your home, with none of the risks or potential hassles of running a generator, such as dangerous carbon monoxide gas from exhaust fumes and dealing with fuel and oil.

Sources indicate that A portable power station’s maximum output tells you the total watts it can produce, which determines what you can and can’t power with it. Look for a power station that can handle the combined wattage of the electronics you plan to plug into it.

Recent findings suggest that some power stations also have surge power that allows them to produce higher wattage for short bursts. This is designed specifically for appliances that draw more watts (known as starting watts) in the first few seconds when you first start them up, including power tools, refrigerators, blenders, and window air conditioners.

A portable power station’s capacity, listed in watt-hours (Wh), determines how much energy a power station can deliver over time. Generally, power stations with more watt-hours can run for longer, but exactly how long depends on the amount of watts the devices connected to the power station draw. You can roughly estimate how long a power station will last by dividing the total watt-hours by the watts drawn (Wh ÷ W = Hrs).

For example, if you have a power station with 2,048-watt-hour capacity and are consistently drawing 400 watts of power: 2,048 ÷ 400 = 5.12 hours of runtime.

It has been revealed that keep in mind that the usable watt-hours are not the same as the watt-hours listed on the power station’s label. You’ll typically get about 85 percent of the listed watt-hours due to power lost in connections and the electricity that the power station itself uses to power its inverter and display. Given those losses, expect to get about 85 percent of a power station’s listed watt-hours in usable power. So, a fully charged 2,000-watt-hour power station will typically give you about 1,700 watt-hours of usable power.

In a recent development, these days, most portable power stations, including all those we recommend here, use LiFePO4 batteries, which are capable of holding far more cycles, which is the number of times a battery goes through a complete discharge and recharge, than older lithium-ion batteries, while also being less likely to combust. Their one drawback is that they have a lower energy density, which means it takes more LiFePO4 batteries than lithium-ion batteries to produce the same amount of power. Still, this is the battery type of choice for portable power stations, both large and small.

In a recent development, while all these power stations are portable, some are easier to transport than others. A power station’s portability is directly related to its power capacity and output.

Small power stations with around 300 watt-hours of capacity and a max output of 300 watts typically weigh under 10 pounds and are about the size of a lunch box.

Midsize models like the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 portable power station, which have a max wattage of between 2,000 and 2,600 watts and a 2,000-watt-hour capacity, are about the size of the printer in your home office and weigh around 60 pounds, just small and light enough for one person to carry from one room to another.

Recent findings suggest that large portable models can weigh up to 135 pounds and are about the size of a suitcase. While these monsters are too large for one person to lift, they do sit on wheels that allow you to move them over flat surfaces, technically making them portable.

In a recent development, portable power stations have an array of output ports, including USB-C, USB-A, car accessory, AC, and RV. Consider what types of appliances or electronics you’re planning to charge and the type of connections they use when choosing a portable power station.

Since the wattage of the output can vary, also consider the maximum charging output of each port to avoid disappointing recharge times. For example, a power station with a USB-C port that has a 15-watt max output will take a much longer time to charge a laptop than one with a 140-watt USB-C port.

If you’re looking for a large-capacity power station that will back up critical circuits in your home or power an RV, you’ll need a station that features a single 30-amp connection that can connect to an RV input or transfer switch.

Portable power stations have control panels with LED displays and buttons that turn inputs off and on and display usage and remaining power. Most portable power stations are also compatible with Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, allowing you to monitor and control them remotely from a smartphone app.

It has been revealed that often, what makes a power station great is the kind of software it includes and what features it offers to help you best manage your power station. For example, some stations that you leave plugged into a wall—so that they stay charged and at the ready—will automatically only recharge your station during low-peak hours when rates may be lower from your electric utility. Features like this one can be incredibly helpful when trying to get the most from your station.

It has been revealed that most large power stations, including the EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus and Anker F3800 Plus, can serve as a UPS (uninterruptible power supply) for your home. To use these power stations as a UPS, plug them into the wall, then plug whatever devices you want backed up into the station’s AC output ports. When the power is on, those devices use energy from the grid. When there is a power outage, the power station instantly switches these devices to battery power. If you live in an area prone to power outages, this can be useful to prevent data loss from a connected computer, keep medical devices running, or run the pump and filter on a fish tank.

Portable power stations heat up when operating for extended periods or when they’re providing power for multiple devices. Internal fans will kick on to keep the power station from overheating. While these fans are far quieter than the roar of a gas-powered generator, they do still create some noise. Smaller power stations are about as loud as a small fan, while larger ones produce about the same amount of noise as a refrigerator.

It has been revealed that A portable power station’s lifespan depends on the type of battery inside. Most newly introduced portable power stations, including all the models we recommend here, feature LiFePO4 battery technology, which lasts far longer than older lithium-ion technology.

How much more? LiFePO4 power stations will last for more than 3,000 charge cycles, or about 10 years. That’s far longer than the 500 or so charge cycles and 3 to 5 years you’ll get from an older power station with a lithium-ion battery.

That depends on the capacity of your portable power station, the wattage of your solar panels, and the weather. To figure that out, divide the station’s total capacity by the total input power of the solar panels (Wh ÷ W = Hrs).

For example, a 1,000-watt-hour power station that’s receiving a consistent stream of 200 watts of power from a solar panel would take about 5 hours to recharge. Keep in mind, this is assuming uninterrupted, direct sunlight conditions, which, even then, may produce varied results.

According to recent reports, some power stations have ingress protection (IP) ratings, indicating they have been tested for water and dust resistance. The Bluetti Elite 200, for example, has an IP65 rating, which means it can withstand water sprays from all angles. However, other portable power stations do not have a weather rating, so it’s vital to check if you plan on using your power station outdoors. Regardless, it’s a good idea to protect your power station from any water or severe weather conditions as much as possible.

Industry News: Trump administration ups ante on aviation funds after ground stop

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21.
  • Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they remarked old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.
  • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they remarked old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.

The increased allotment, which the administration officials didn’t fully flesh out, comes after the nation’s air traffic control system experienced “instability” in its radar and communications at certain facilities earlier in the day, Duffy told reporters.

He mentioned “inconsistency in the data” being issued by those systems led to implementation of the nationwide ground stop, saying the order was given out of “an abundance of caution” before being lifted about four hours later.

During a Friday night White House briefing, Duffy and Mullin explained the issues were driven by “an incredibly old air traffic control system.”.

Earlier in the day, the stoppage had caused mass confusion and raised questions about potential terror attacks, or artificial intelligence breakouts resulting from fresh software the agency is rolling out. While Mullin remarked “we’re not ruling out anything,” he explained that “the public was never at danger through this process.”.

Still, Duffy called the incident “an emergency” while calling for additional modernization funds.

“This is an emergency,” he mentioned. “I want $50 billion. President Trump is a builder. He’s going to build this network and deliver for the American people. But the president can’t deliver for America unless the Congress delivers the money to make it happen.”.

The latest figure is $19.1 billion higher than the figure Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought called on congressional appropriators to approve in a Thursday letter.

Mullin said the fresh $50 billion figure was an administration estimate for a “complete overhaul of the system” which has been going through a “patchwork” upgrade process that may have overwhelmed the older equipment still being used.

Industry observers note that “We need someone to come in and build the whole system," Mullin mentioned. "Nickel and diming it together does not work.".

Industry observers note that thursday’s call for $30.1 billion echoes a White House-backed bill that Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., introduced in September, which would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $2 billion for "cloud computing and national airspace system telecommunications.".

Those funds would come after $12.5 billion allocated to the effort through the July 2025 reconciliation law that Duffy and Vought called a “down-payment.".

According to recent reports, senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee Republicans touted those already-appropriated funds in a social media post. They pointed to $1.9 billion provided in the reconciliation law that would go toward upgrading air route traffic control centers, which guide planes across long distances after departure and which the FAA had cited as the cause of the problem.

Recent findings suggest that the 22 air route traffic control centers across the country guide aircraft using instrument-dependent flight prepares. Under such plans, pilots use instruments, electronic navigation and air traffic control assistance to guide them and maintain separation from other aircraft in certain airspaces.

The committee’s majority mentioned Friday's outage highlighted the need to prioritize modernization of the air route traffic control centers, arguing that President Lyndon B. Johnson was in office the last time a fresh one was built.

Commerce ranking member Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., stated in a statement Friday night that the panel is looking into FAA and airspace telecommunications issues.

“Technology issues related to how planes communicate through primary frequencies, backup frequencies, and other issues will be something the Commerce Committee will be reviewing,” Cantwell mentioned.

Cantwell is poised to take the committee's gavel come January as Democrats assume the majority in the Senate.

In a joint statement Friday night, House Transportation and Infrastructure Chairman Sam Graves, R-Mo., and ranking member Rick Larsen, D-Wash., called the communication failures “concerning” and remarked their committee would “thoroughly review the issues that led to this nationwide ground stop.”.

Both committees have also been in monthslong negotiations over dueling aviation safety bills responding to the January 2025 midair collision near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport that killed 67 people.

Recent findings suggest that at issue in those negotiations is which location transmission technology should be mandated to aid in air traffic control operations and allow aircraft to maintain appropriate distance. Leaders have remarked they hope to reach a deal in the lame-duck session.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Holland America Line unveiled its 2028-29 Asia cruise season, marking the Eurodam’s debut in the region.

The season will run from September 2028 through May 2029, with itineraries ranging from 11 to 27 days.

Departing from Tokyo, Japan; Hong Kong, China; and Singapore, they will take guests to Japan, South Korea, China, Taiwan, the Philippines and Southeast Asia.

“Asia is one of those regions where you can experience something completely different from one port to the next, from a major city like Hong Kong to our new call at Coron in the Philippines, known for its turquoise waters and rich history,” mentioned Paul Grigsby, vice president of deployment and revenue planning for Holland America Line.

Recent findings suggest that “That contrast is what makes these itineraries so interesting to build. The upcoming ports take guests beyond the places they may already know, introducing them to islands, coastlines and historic communities that reveal another side of the region, while natural phenomena like Japan’s cherry blossoms can make the experience completely different depending on when you visit.”.

Five latest ports will be featured: Coron, Busuanga Island, Philippines, Hirara and Wakayama in Japan, Magong in Taiwan and Muara, a gateway to Brunei Darussalam.

Across the season, guests can enjoy overnight stays and late-night departures in 14 ports throughout the region, including two new ones Keelung (Taipei) and Phú Mỹ (Ho Chi Minh City).

In a recent development, as recently declared, there will also be a 27-day Coffee, Tea & Spice Route Legendary Voyage, departing Jan. 3 roundtrip from Singapore.

The Destination Dining program will bring the itinerary onboard, allowing guests to sample dishes including Japanese rockfish and fresh sushi, Korean bibimbap with beef bulgogi, Thai mango sticky rice, Filipino chicken adobo, and more.

For a limited time, when guests book 2028-2029 Asia cruises with the Have It All premium package, the standard package amenities of shore excursions, specialty dining, a Signature Beverage Package and Surf Wi-Fi are included.

There is also the added perk of free prepaid crew appreciation, along with free upgrades to the Elite Beverage Package and Premium Wi-Fi.

Guests can also take advantage of the Exclusive Mariner Society Early Booking Bonus and Mariner Society loyalty members can get up to $400 onboard credit per stateroom.

The 7 Best Fireproof Home Safes Protect Your Valuables from Extreme Heat
