Breaking: The Secret Reason Why Ancient Roman Concrete Is So Remarkably Strong—And How One Engineer Has Recreated It

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1029 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.
  • The Pantheon, Rome’s unreinforced concrete dome, constructed around 118 to 125 C.E., still stands intact to this day.
  • According to recent reports, for decades, researchers credited the inclusion of volcanic ash from Pozzuoli, a city in Naples, Italy, for the unique strength in the mix; others claimed that lime, a calcium oxide or calcium hydroxide binder created from heating limestone, was the key ingredient.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

The Pantheon, Rome’s unreinforced concrete dome, constructed around 118 to 125 C.E., still stands intact to this day. The Aqua Virgo, part of the ancient Roman system of aqueducts, was built in 19 B.C.E., yet still supplies Roman fountains, including Trevi, today. Is it any wonder that ancient Rome still draws our global admiration?

According to recent reports, for decades, researchers credited the inclusion of volcanic ash from Pozzuoli, a city in Naples, Italy, for the unique strength in the mix; others claimed that lime, a calcium oxide or calcium hydroxide binder created from heating limestone, was the key ingredient. Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s Admir Masic, a civil and environmental engineering professor, thought there must be more to the story.

Masic established a lab at MIT with the specific goal of researching ancient Roman concrete. First and foremost a chemist, he claims he knew there was something beneath the surface of Roman concrete potentially lending it strength. His team of researchers, from MIT, Harvard, Italy, and Switzerland, discovered that ancient Roman concrete gets its strength—and therefore its incredible longevity—from its inherent self-healing properties. As cracks form, the surrounding material somehow fills them back in, over and over.

In a recent development, scientists commonly suspected that ash, and not lime, was the hero of the Roman concrete-making process, because the Romans were the first to add volcanic ash to the mixture. This hydration-based method gives the mixture additional strength and makes it possible to build in all seasons.

It has been revealed that but it didn’t explain the self-healing quality. Another mystery was in the concrete’s apparent crystalline phases, known to take shape only at high temperatures—at least 80 degrees Celsius (or about 176 degrees Fahrenheit). Yet, the Romans wouldn’t have exposed their concrete mixture to those sorts of temperatures.

Industry observers note that then, researchers discovered calcium aluminate hydrate being used as a binding agent in ancient Roman concrete, which only created further intrigue. This is where the mystery of self-healing gained its first substantial clue—trying to learn where the calcium came from, Masic claims. So his team’s focus shifted to the overlooked role of lime, which is primarily composed of calcium compounds.

Industry observers note that masic notes that modern concrete, when mixed with lime, volcanic components, and water, creates a homogeneous mixture—quite unlike ancient Roman concrete, which is studded with tiny, distinct white particles. “How is it possible that every construction site would make this heterogeneous material even though they put so much effort [into] making it very standard in terms of ingredients [and] how to mix it?” Masic wondered.

The research team decided to investigate the mechanical, structural, and chemical properties of these particles, dubbed “lime clasts,” which were present in every sample they analyzed, Masic says. It led the team to realize “that lime clasts are not an error in mixing, or sloppy mixing, but they are the root of a very specific way of mixing mortars.” Not present in modern concrete, but ubiquitous in the ancient Roman version.

Industry observers note that originally, researchers believed that the Romans added water to the lime mixture to make a slurry. This “slaking” creates a homogeneously structured mixture. However, the presence of the lime clasts didn’t fit into this model.

What the Romans actually did was “hot mixing,” which introduces a novel series of chemical reactions. They ground the stone into tiny pieces of calcium oxide and mixed them with volcanic ash and a dry aggregate. Finally, they added water. “This is where the reaction of calcium oxide with water happens, and the entire mix gets hot, [which] releases energy, and creates hot spots up to 200 to 250 degrees Celsius,” Masic explains.

Industry observers note that while lime and the ash formed the basis of the mixture, the constellation of millimeter-scale, mineral particles embedded throughout the mortar turned out to be the secret outcome of the hot mixing process. The key to hot mixing is that it doesn’t dissolve all of the lime clasts. Instead, they get systematically embedded into the concrete mix, creating a reservoir of calcium. When the concrete is exposed to water, the calcium spontaneously expands, creating a protective layer of nanoparticles that fill in the cracks before they can spread. Voila, self-healing concrete. Masic’s team published their findings in the journal Science Advances.

Sources indicate that the team’s own recreation of Roman concrete healed a crack within two weeks. A modern concrete mixture didn’t heal at all, allowing water to flow through the crack. Eventually, water seepage like this destroys the integrity of modern concrete structures.

Roman self-healing concrete allows the mixture to last longer and requires less maintenance and less new material for construction—which also reduces emissions during concrete production. Standard cement production, the solid binder in concrete, accounts for about 8 percent of global CO2 emissions today.

It has been revealed that our world actually has various forms of self-healing concrete, such as bioconcrete, in which bacterial spores activate and produce calcium carbonate to fill in cracks. However, the high costs of modern methods keep the industry from using them widely, says Masic. Meanwhile the ancient Roman method offers “self-healing at an extremely competitive price,” he says.

Now that we know the secret, should we return to making concrete this way?

In fact, Masic co-founded a firm in 2021, that uses lessons he has learned from studying ancient Roman concrete. Today, DMAT is creating a concrete additive “that increases the lifespan of concrete structures by 50 percent and reduces CO2 emissions to 40% of traditional concrete,” according to MIT’s Climate Portal. As of August 2026, their material is part of underground water tanks, road barriers, and pavement in Italy and Switzerland. DMAT also intends to expand to U.S. infrastructure projects.

Manasee Wagh contributed to this story.

His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Judge Frederico dos Santos Messias of the São Paulo State Court of Justice’s specialized maritime court granted the request from R11 Travel Viagens e Turismo against GLCL Global Cruiseline Ltd., the Cyprus-registered tech giant that operates as Corazul.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A Brazilian court ordered the arrest of Corazul’s the Buenavista at the Port of Santos after the cruise line’s exclusive Brazilian distributor claimed it was owed about $270,000 (R$1.48 million), according to a court decision dated Nov. 13.

Judge Frederico dos Santos Messias of the São Paulo State Court of Justice’s specialized maritime court granted the request from R11 Travel Viagens e Turismo against GLCL Global Cruiseline Ltd., the Cyprus-registered tech giant that operates as Corazul.

The judge issued the order without first hearing from Corazul, the decision demonstrated.

In a recent development, the order barred the Buenavista from leaving Brazilian waters. The court noted the ship was anchored off Santos for repairs.

The judge set security at about $323,000 (R$1.78 million) and remarked the ship would be released if Corazul deposited that amount or posted a bank guarantee.

According to the decision, R11 remarked Corazul owed about $1.27 million (R$6.96 million) under a four-year exclusive distribution agreement signed in March. That figure included about $780,000 (EUR 675,000) in unpaid quarterly marketing contributions. After subtracting about $1 million (R$5.48 million) in passenger funds it held, R11 put the net balance at about $270,000.

The filing, as summarized by the court, described a series of disruptions including the cancellation of the Buenavista’s European season in June; the cancellation of its Oct. 23 inaugural Brazilian cruise nine days before departure and complaints about onboard service on the Oct. 30 sailing. The firm has since suspended operations and R11 has stopped selling cruises on the ship.

According to recent reports, R11 noted Corazul demanded $400,000 on Nov. 4 before it would operate the Nov. 6 departure. R11 refused.

The court noted that only two of the 11 sailings scheduled between Oct. 23 and Nov. 27 operated. Corazul also suspended operations until Nov. 30 and moved the end of its Brazil season up to March 5, 2027. The judge wrote that Corazul’s own communications indicated a “serious liquidity collapse.”.

In a recent development, the dispute is headed to arbitration in São Paulo under AMCHAM, the American Chamber of Commerce for Brazil. The decision stated that R11 must file within 30 days or the order lapses. Corazul has five days after being served to contest it.

#54194. The 8 Best Home Generators Are a Significant Investment. These Deliver Reliable Power During an Outage.

📅 07 Nov 2018 • ⏱️ 25m • 📚 Deep Dive (4924 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popularmechanics ↗ Open Full Page

The 8 Best Home Generators Are a Significant Investment. These Deliver Reliable Power During an Outage.

📅 07 Nov 2018 | ⏱️ 25 min read (4924 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~25 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Stronger and more frequent severe weather events are making a compelling argument for investing in a home generator.
  • It has been revealed that the term “home generator” can be confusing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Stronger and more frequent severe weather events are making a compelling argument for investing in a home generator. A large portable generator or a permanently installed standby generator can keep your entire home powered and operational for several days, or at least keep a few critical appliances such as a refrigerator running until the power comes back on. The cost of emergency power is never a small investment, though it is an increasingly important one.

It has been revealed that the term “home generator” can be confusing. It’s an unofficial category that includes larger portable generators capable of powering several appliances or a few critical circuits using a transfer switch (not all portable generators are built for this task). It also includes permanently installed standby generators that can automatically switch to whole-home backup power when the lights go out. Choosing the right size generator primarily comes down to how much power you think you’ll need in an emergency.

There are many reliable home generators that deliver a great deal of power. Some offer you the choice of running on multiple different fuels, while other models use an inverter that can give you quieter and “cleaner” operation. There is a nice range of prices available, too, so you can easily find a generator below that fits your needs as well as your budget.

For the generators on this list that we tested, we considered the difficulty of unboxing, assembling, and starting each generator for the first time, because few things are as frustrating as buying a tool that turns out to be unnecessarily complicated from the get-go.

It has been revealed that once set up, the generators we reviewed were subjected to different load conditions, including things such as power tools, home appliances, and even recharging large power stations. We assessed the features that distinguish these generators from each other, including safety features, app connectivity, and portability, among other things.

A few picks on our list have not been tested, but we included them here after considerable research, taking into account the brand’s reputation, our knowledge of its product lines, various outside reviews, and our own experience testing similar models from those same brands.

Industry observers note that the DuroMax XP11000iH is a powerful midsize dual-fuel inverter generator, capable of keeping most homes up and running for an extended period of time. Inverter generators are a step above traditional generators because they convert alternating current (AC) to direct current (DC) and then back again to AC. This process creates cleaner, more efficient power and enables the generator to run more quietly and fuel efficiently.

According to recent reports, having two fuel options—gas and propane—provides a significant boost of convenience by allowing you to use whatever’s handy. No gasoline? You can use the same tank of propane you use for your gas grill. It’s also parallel-capable, so you can daisy-chain it with another generator if you need extra power.

The generator is enclosed in a large, sturdy plastic casing, which makes it durable and provides a fair amount of sound dampening. Of the many gas generators I’ve tested, it may be the quietest model that’s capable of backing up a whole home, especially when it’s running on propane, which trims it down by another few decibels. At 61 decibels on a 20 percent load, it’s about as loud as a dishwasher. Most comparably sized generators go up to around 80 decibels—about the same volume as a police siren.

According to recent reports, in addition to a full suite of essential modern safety features such as a carbon monoxide shutoff and low-oil shutoff, it goes the extra mile with lots of little touches, like remote start. The integrated battery tender keeps it ready to start, no matter how long it’s been sitting, which can be a lifesaver, too. When you do run out to check it, an onboard display shows you key stats such as hours run, current load, and voltage output.

According to recent reports, the only downside I could find was its weight. At upward of 200 pounds, it isn’t easy to carry. It does have wheels and sturdy handles, though, so it isn’t hard to wheel around on flat, paved ground—if you can push a loaded wheelbarrow, you can push this. Not that you’ll need to move it much; it’s a very sturdy generator, and it comes assembled with the wheels and handles attached (not all generators come with those pre-attached). —Reviewed by Nick Hilden.

Technically, there are cheaper generators out there, but the Generac GP9500E offers an outstanding blend of capability, quality, and durability at a very reasonable price. As such, this is where I’d steer you if you’re trying to shave down your spend.

Its 9,500-watt running capacity is slightly higher than the DuroMax’s, and it’s capable of powering all but the largest of homes. It can get a little noisy under a heavy load, but that’s common with units this size. It let out a relatively moderate purr when it was just powering the lights and a few appliances, but it became more of a roar when the heat kicked on.

With three fuel options—gas, propane, and natural gas—you get about as much versatility as you could possibly expect from a generator. A relatively large 7.5-gallon gas tank delivers a long runtime between fill-ups. And, while I was initially skeptical as to the necessity of the third fuel option, having natural gas support showed its value when a storm knocked out the power, and I didn’t have gas or propane on hand. All I needed to do was plug it into the natural gas line, and suddenly my house was the only one on the block with lights on.

Sources indicate that beyond that, though, it’s a fairly basic model. It has essential safety features such as low-oil and CO shutdown, but lacks elements such as a fancy digital display, remote start, or app. I don’t necessarily think that’s a problem: It can be helpful to get a piece of machinery that doesn’t go overboard with features. Its control panel is about as straightforward as can be, and it’s a cinch to get up and running.

It has been revealed that like my top pick, the GP9500E is exceedingly heavy. It’s also quite sturdy, though, which feels like a fair trade. The outlet covers aren’t as flimsy and breakable as with many other models of a similar price point. It isn’t completely immobile: It has wheels and handles that make it easy to cart around short distances. Realistically, though, weight is almost always going to be an issue with any generator capable of backing up your house.

Ultimately, its selling point is the price. It’s hard to find a quality tri-fuel generator for around $1,100, and the GP9500E performs well if you don’t mind losing out on some bells and whistles.

When AC power isn’t available, the greenest way to recharge a power station is with solar panels. However, the panel’s maximum power output often exceeds the maximum solar input, so they just can’t recharge fast enough. In these cases, whole-home, battery-based backup systems need the help of a fuel-based generator to recharge, so you’re not left high and dry if the power’s still out. That’s where the EcoFlow Smart Generator 4000 comes in.

Industry observers note that this dual-fuel (gas or propane) generator connects to select EcoFlow power stations via a DC charging and communication cable, including the Delta Pro, Delta Pro 3, Delta 3, Delta 3 Plus, and Delta 2 Max. (Note: If your preferred brand is Anker, it also makes a fuel generator that’s compatible with some of its power stations, the 5500 Tri-Fuel Inverter Generator, which we also tested and reviewed.) This DC connection allows autonomous operation, so when a station’s battery hits critically low levels, the generator automatically starts to recharge it.

You can also recharge non-DC-compatible power stations by simply plugging them into the AC output, though it’s a slower recharge. If it’s an EcoFlow station, you can still automate startup, too, by pairing over Bluetooth. But you won’t be able to do this with other brands of power stations.

Our test editor Bradley Ford noted that EcoFlow’s app is one of the best features of this generator. Connecting over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, he used it to monitor fuel consumption and output, as well as set automated functions. He also tested how it can set the charging speed, monitor power output, and schedule times to start and stop the generator. He especially liked that the app provides a lot of useful information as well, such as generator fuel usage and estimated runtime.

Of course, it can work as a standalone generator, too, though there are some limitations. Ford notes that there are only two outlets: a 120-volt, 20-amp outlet and a 120-volt, 30-amp outlet. The latter outlet can connect to a manual transfer switch installed in your home, but it won’t be able to power any 240-volt circuits, and the total output of 3,200 watts is only enough to power a few circuits. However, he thinks it would work well for RV use, and because it’s an inverter generator, it’s better at safely powering sensitive electronics like TVs and computers. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford.

Full EcoFlow Dual-Fuel Smart Generator 4000 Review.

In a recent development, whether you’re connecting devices individually, powering an RV, or running home backup power during a storm, this generator from Westinghouse (model WGen9500DF) covers all the bases. In addition to being dual-fuel (gas or propane), it includes both 30- and 50-amp outputs capable of powering 120- and 240-volt circuits. That means you could connect this generator to a transfer switch installed in your home using either option. And with 9,500 running watts of power, it’s enough for several critical circuits in your home, including the ones that run on 240 volts, such as a heating/ventilation/air-conditioning system, electric dryer, or well pump.

Several other features caught our attention, including a push-button electric start and stop (no need to mess with a pull cable), plus a remote start key fob. There’s an automatic low-oil shutoff, and the display provides the voltage output, frequency, and lifetime hours (this can run up to 12 hours on a 6.6-gallon tank of gasoline). The only drawback is the 74-decibel noise level. While that’s typical of generators of this type, if you're planning on using this to power an RV or camper, it may be too loud for some parks, as many limit generator noise to under 70 decibels.

Recent findings suggest that while it does not offer as much power as some of the choices on our list, Champion’s 4,750-watt generator has enough capacity to run three or four critical 120-volt circuits in your home during an outage. It will also power small to medium campers and RVs via a dedicated 30-amp, 120-volt RV receptacle. Listed at around $600, this generator gives you a lot for the price you pay.

In a recent development, this generator uses a 224-cc engine with a 4.7-gallon fuel tank, enabling it to run for up to 14 hours (up to 10 hours using propane). A gauge displays a readout of the runtime hours and voltage output, and there’s an automated shutoff feature if the oil starts to run low. Since it’s dual-fuel, this generator can run off propane in addition to gasoline. For instance, if you are using it with an RV, you can run it off a camper’s propane tank without having to pack and haul a gas can. Likewise, with the included adapter hose, you can hook it up to a 20-pound propane tank.

Sources indicate that there are a few drawbacks. Beyond the somewhat low wattage output for whole-home backup, there are no 240-volt outlets, so if you need that many volts to power circuits in your home for something such as a dryer or water heater, this model won’t be right for you. But if you just need something to keep some lights on and run a few appliances, this generator will get the job done and not cost you a ton of money up front to do it. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford.

Industry observers note that there are many reasons to opt for an inverter generator, but the two biggest ones are: cleaner, more stable power (important for powering electronics safely) and less noise. Loudness becomes a major factor with larger generators, as more power requires a more powerful engine. That’s why we were so impressed with this model (EU7000iS) from Honda. It delivers a lot of power but at notably low loudness levels.

It’s crucial to note that this is not a small generator. It weighs in at 263 pounds, making it one of the heaviest on our list. That noted, we found it fairly comfortable to move around. The metal frame that houses the generator has a folding handle that locks into place and is capped with soft grips, while on the front of the frame there are strong 10-inch rubber wheels. This made it fairly easy to roll around, even up some gradual slopes.

It’s also quite sturdy. The outer casing is constructed of stamped metal and impact-resistant composite hard plastic, with two large, hinged maintenance doors that lock into place.

Once we fired up the generator, it was noticeably quieter than other models we’ve tested, even when outputting a 60 percent load. Using an app-based sound meter, we were reading around 70 decibels from 15 feet away, which is lower than you would see with a non-inverter generator. This is helped by an “Eco Throttle” mode that adjusts the engine speed to meet demand as different devices are added, but we found even the standard throttle mode was fairly quiet as well.

Other things we liked were an app that allows for remote operation over Bluetooth, ground fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) protection, a carbon monoxide (CO) sensor, and 240-volt output over a 30-amp connection, which will let the generator connect to a manual transfer switch for sending direct power to your home electrical box.

The two downsides are the cost (it’s very expensive at more than $4,000) and the fact that it can only be powered by gasoline; Honda doesn’t offer dual- or tri-fuel models for using propane or natural gas. But if those two considerations don’t bother you, the EU7000iS Inverter Generator is a high-quality machine that will keep you more quietly powered than some of the competition.

Full Honda EU7000iS 7000-Watt Inverter Generator Review.

In a recent development, battery-based backup systems are getting smarter and more powerful every year, making them an increasingly strong contender to fuel-based standby generators. This model from EcoFlow is one of the most powerful we’ve tested.

The power station combines a separate inverter unit with two 6-kilowatt-hour batteries for a total of 12-kilowatt-hour capacity. That’s enough to run power-hungry devices simultaneously—things such as heating/ventilation/air-conditioning systems, electric ovens and dryers, microwaves, and air-conditioning units. Add to this increased solar input, and you can recharge faster, too. For our tests, we connected this to a home electrical system in the home using EcoFlow’s Smart Home Panel 3, which acts as the automatic transfer switch.

During testing, our reviewer experienced two power outages, one for a few seconds and one for several minutes. This power station features an Emergency Power Supply (EPS) mode, which facilitates a 20-millisecond switch to backup power—without this set, it normally switches in about five seconds. During the longer outage, the switch from grid to backup power, and then back again, was seamless. It was fast enough that the lights never flickered and the internet never dropped.

In a recent development, several advanced smart features stand out. The smartphone app enables you to view power usage, down to the circuit, preset what circuits get backup power during outages, manually turn circuits on and off, and schedule automated tasks such as charging and discharging. You’ll also receive notifications when the grid goes down and the backup power takes over. If you live in an area where electricity is cheaper during low-peak hours, it can also prioritize recharging from grid power by choosing those times of day.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, this system is highly expandable. You can add up to eight more batteries for a total of 10, and an inlet box that comes with the smart panel has three ports. You could plug a Delta Pro Ultra X, bolstered by extra batteries, into each port to increase the total energy storage up to a whopping 184.3 kilowatt-hours of capacity and 36 kilowatts of continuous output.

One of the biggest things our reviewer appreciates about the Delta Pro Ultra X and Smart Home Panel 3 is the peace of mind it gives. If the grid goes down, they know that their home systems will continue to run. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford.

Recent findings suggest that pulsar is a relatively new brand in the generator business and doesn’t have a long track record. We first spotted it on Amazon and didn’t seriously consider its generators for testing. That was, up until our test editor needed a generator (with specific features and on a budget) after a generator failed at his solar-powered off-grid cabin. Happily, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel Inverter Generator showed up quickly and didn’t disappoint.

The generator was easy to assemble and prep, taking only 15 minutes. After adding oil, it was connected to a propane cylinder and was up and running on the first cycle of the starter. Our first task was to charge a solar battery bank during a wintertime period when there was not enough available sunlight, and it worked perfectly.

Industry observers note that we have logged more than 20 hours of use so far, running it primarily on propane connected to a 100-pound cylinder (enough fuel to last a couple of months). This Pulsar puts out very clean power, with a claimed total harmonic distortion (THD) of less than 3 percent, which met the requirements of the solar inverter-charger I was using. Using the inverter to monitor the current frequency, we found that it was indeed very stable with minimal variance, between 59.97 and 60.09 Hz. All things considered, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel is a good value for the specs, capacity, and features. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford.

Recent findings suggest that true whole-home backup requires a professionally installed standby generator like Generac’s 22-kilowatt home standby generator. It’s designed to power a house that’s roughly 2,500 square feet. If you need to run specialized medical devices, work from home, or have kids who are learning from home, this model is a sound investment.

Another benefit of this bundle is that it includes a transfer switch, which is required if you’re planning to install this type of generator. It supports 200-amp electrical service, providing the backup circuits needed to power high-voltage appliances such as refrigerators and well pumps, along with air conditioning and heating systems. Plus, there’s built-in WiFi for checking the status of your generator and receiving maintenance alerts when you’re not at home.

You could just drive over to your local hardware store and buy a large portable generator to use as a home backup, but we wouldn’t recommend it. You want to make sure you’re getting a generator that can back up your home and power all the appliances, lights, and electronics inside. (Plus some extra watts in case you need them down the line.).

In addition, there are often state and local laws or homeowners association rules and restrictions around using them in residential neighborhoods. Choosing poorly or setting up your backup generator incorrectly could damage the generator or short out your house power at best, or lead to fire, electrocution, or carbon monoxide poisoning at worst.

Picking the best generator for your home starts with a little math. Ideally, you want to calculate how much energy you need to keep your house running, and buy a generator that can handle everything you want to power in an emergency, with room to spare.

The two key specs to pay attention to are the running wattage and starting wattage (e.g., 9,500 running watts / 12,500 starting watts). Running wattage is effectively your generator’s capacity: It tells you how much power a generator can produce steadily without any possibility of an overload. Starting wattage is the generator’s max output, or how much power it can produce for short, peak bursts when appliances first switch on.

When you are making your list, note what items are 120-volt and which ones are 240-volt appliances. It’s not hard to identify them. Refrigerators, small appliances, and most electronics run on 120-volt power and plug into standard outlets. Anything that requires 240 volts—electric dryers, well pumps, and HVAC systems—is either hardwired into your electrical system or has a dedicated 240-volt outlet. If you need to power the latter, the installation of a transfer switch and a generator that outputs at least 30 amps/240 volts may be required.

It has been revealed that if you’re just looking to keep the fridge, lights, and a few modest appliances going through a short blackout, you can usually get away with a generator that supplies 3,000 to 5,000 watts. If you want to run the heat, hot water, and several appliances at once, blueprint on using at least 6,000 to 8,000 watts. If you think you’re going to be adding large appliances such as laundry machines and dishwashers, expect to need 10,000 watts or more.

A piece of advice we have: Once you figure out how much you need, opt for buying a generator that outputs around 20 percent more than that. It’s not uncommon to realize you need more than you thought you would.

It has been revealed that it’s also important to consider that, while generators are certainly a hefty investment, they usually stand the test of time. Consumer-grade portable generators can run anywhere from 1,000 to 3,000 hours, sometimes more. If you run one for 100 hours per year, it should last for 10 to 30 years.

There are four basic types of generators, each with advantages and disadvantages.

Sources indicate that the most traditional of the generator category, these run on carbon-based fuels like gasoline, propane, and natural gas. Some allow you to switch between them. Dual-fuel models add the option of either propane or natural gas, while tri-fuel versions offer all three fuel options. These generators can be small, offering as little as 1,000 watts of power output, or run very large, as much as 20,000 watts or more.

Different fuels offer different power capabilities. For example, a tri-fuel generator may offer 9,500 running watts and 12,500 starting watts with gasoline, but only 8,500/11,200 with propane and 7,500/9,500 with natural gas. Regardless of the fuel you choose, this type of generator must always be operated 5 to 20 feet away from the home or any window or door, because the carbon monoxide exhaust is deadly. Even a garage with an open door is not safe.

Industry observers note that often this type of generator is called portable, but that's a relative term: Almost all of them weigh more than 100 pounds, and many are upwards of 200. Many are on wheels, making them relatively easy to store in a garage and wheel outside when you need them, but actually moving one will likely require at least two people.

Inverter generators look and operate the same as other portable generators, but have an added component–a power inverter– that converts the alternating current (AC) power generated by its fuel source to DC (Direct Current), then inverts it back to AC before putting it out.

According to recent reports, generators without an inverter generate varying degrees of distortion in the sine wave of the alternating current, which can trigger power surges and other complications in some electronics. The inverter stabilizes the power, almost like a filter, “cleaning” it for more sensitive electronics like TVs and laptops.

It has been revealed that so why doesn’t every generator have an inverter? Inverters are expensive, so the generators are, too.

Realistically speaking, you don’t need an inverter generator to power major appliances and your house power, but if you’re running a full home backup (or if you count a TV or laptop among your essential electronics), holding out for an inverter is a smart move.

Recent findings suggest that while often referred to as “solar generators” because they can be paired with solar panels, power stations are not really true generators. They're advanced battery banks that store power, which you precharge using AC power or solar panels. They can’t generate electricity in real time.

But because they can offer many of the same electrical outputs as a fuel generator, they can function similarly to a traditional generator for as long as the batteries retain a charge. Some stations are very small and meant only for off-grid adventures like camping trips, but some are large enough to run whole-home systems that can produce 14,400 watts or more with expandable batteries.

Since power stations don't run on fuel or have an engine, they can be used indoors without the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning and operate with almost no noise.

Recent findings suggest that the downside is that once the power is depleted, the power station must be recharged. If the power grid is still unavailable, it can take many hours in ideal sunny conditions if all you have are solar panels. You can use a traditional generator to recharge a power station, but some may view that as defeating the purpose.

In a recent development, standby generators are permanently installed generators designed to automatically take over for your house power in the event of an outage. You can set them to power your whole house, or only specific circuits, giving you precise control. Standby generators start at around 10,000 watts (10 kilowatts) but can go up to much higher. For the average home, a range of 10 to 25 kilowatts is usually enough.

They typically require professional installation, making them the most costly option. Since many large portable generators can effectively back up a house for a few hours for a lot less money, standby models are still considered a more niche option.

In a recent development, when you draw too much power from your generator, its performance will start to decline. At home, your lights will start to dim or flicker, and appliances may turn off momentarily. The generator itself may also start to get louder, or sound like it’s working extra hard to keep up.

If you notice these signs, start turning off and unplugging non-essential power sources immediately, or turn the generator off entirely for ten minutes or so to reduce the power load.

Sources indicate that this is an urgent problem, so do not wait to take action: If you overwork your generator for too long, it’s only a matter of time before it starts to overheat, produce smoke, or break down. The damage from an extended overload could permanently damage the generator or, worse, start a fire.

With the right size for your home, a portable or standby generator can run as long as you keep feeding it fuel and stay within its running wattage capacity; however, you should not run them indefinitely. Manufacturers recommend you allow them to rest for 30 minutes or more after at least 24 hours of use. Check the manual of your generator for its specific recommendations.

You will get more time from each tank of gas if you draw less power, so it helps to pay extra attention to your electricity usage when you’re running the generator.

It has been revealed that make sure to turn your gas and/or propane generators off when it’s time to refill the tank. Failing to do so could lead to a fire.

Power stations, since they rely on electricity or solar power, can almost always be charged while in use.

Sources indicate that never run a fuel-based generator (gasoline, propane, natural gas) indoors. Burning fuel releases carbon monoxide (CO), which will rapidly build up to deadly levels in an enclosed space.

It has been revealed that set your generator up outside, between 5 and 20 feet away from your home and/or any garages, sheds, or other walls. Position it as far as possible from doors, windows, and vents, with the exhaust positioned away from the house, to minimize the possibility of fumes wafting in. If you keep it outside all year round, find a naturally covered position where snow won’t naturally pile up around it.

Recent findings suggest that my generator is situated near my home’s power box, which is located on a windowless side of my home. It stands about five feet from the exterior wall, with plenty of space on all sides, but close enough to sit under the roof peak overhang 20 feet above.

David is a Reviews Editor for Hearst’s Enthusiast Group, contributing to Popular Mechanics, Runner’s World, Bicycling, Best Products, and Biography. He has over 25 years of experience writing about and reviewing consumer electronics, kitchen appliances, DIY products, outdoor gear, and more. He also spent years covering the ever-changing world of online retail. To relax, he loves experimenting with new recipes, tweaking his smart home setup, and spending time outdoors on his bike or camping.

#54193. Inside NYC’s Pool Scene, the City’s Great Equalizer

Inside NYC’s Pool Scene, the City’s Great Equalizer

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1803 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Just when we thought Newly introduced York had seen it all, I caught wind that the first-ever five-borough pool tournament—in the city’s history—was about to kick off.
  • Sources indicate that it was all thanks to Dan Tran, the brains behind the Five Boro Break.
  • Dan Tran, the brains behind the Five Boro Break, has been shooting pool across the city for more than a decade.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just when we thought Newly introduced York had seen it all, I caught wind that the first-ever five-borough pool tournament—in the city’s history—was about to kick off.

Sources indicate that it was all thanks to Dan Tran, the brains behind the Five Boro Break. Tran has been shooting pool across the city for more than a decade and has played on more than 130 tables out of the 400 to 500 he estimates are in NYC (he even catalogs them out of his own goodwill for other New Yorkers, on Pool Tables NYC). He’s just that guy: an absolute force of nature with a heavy case of do-the-impossible syndrome. One day over summer, at a league night with fellow pool-playing regulars, he wondered if there was a way to get folks like these together for one substantial game—to unite New York’s pool-playing dive bar families and play as one.

Dan Tran, the brains behind the Five Boro Break, has been shooting pool across the city for more than a decade.

In a recent development, the idea was a tournament “built by pool players, run by pool players,” states Tran, who you’ll most often find playing at George & Jacks in Williamsburg. “No money changing hands, no ulterior motive.” Just bringing together this community, which Tran is the first to admit existed long before he stepped on the scene.

So this powerhouse did it: 256 players, 16 venues, all five boroughs, over two days in early November. When I caught up with Tran the week before the tournament, he still couldn’t believe he was bringing the idea to life. “I was like, 'What am I signing up to do once I post this?' But then I posted it, and it just took off—like completely took off. And everybody was like, 'Yeah, we can totally do this.'”.

I rode the wave of Tran’s infectious energy and spent an entire weekend hopping between dives watching the tournament’s pool players do what they do best.

The audience at NYC bar Sugar Mouse applauds Five Boro Break creator Dan Tran at the finals.

On Saturday, November 7, you could feel it in the air. There was something electric about knowing the grittiest corners of Fresh York City were locked in on the same game. That distinct four o’clock autumn sunlight was shining on Bushwick Ice House, one of the 16 venues, when I walked in with Traveler’s Julia Abbonizio and Skyli Alvarez, who were ready to photograph the scene. Gathered around a red-felt table were a dozen or so players who shot us “what’s up” nods as we entered; the bartender moseyed over with “what’s it gonna be?” eyes. Without a word exchanged, we were already part of the bar’s family.

The crowd around us was dressed in their dive-bar best (jeans), and glowing under the neon-red Budweiser lights. The energy in the room matched the game unfolding. One moment, the place roared with Miller High Life clinks and friends catching up. The next it would go pin-drop silent as someone bent over and lined up a shot. More often than not, we’d hear a “nice” before the cue even struck, or a congratulatory clap before someone sank the 8-ball, because everyone knew the game well enough to see exactly what was coming.

Will Pay, a Bushwick Ice House regular, designed the tournament's felt-green shirts.

Satoe Onizuka plays Netta Rawner (left) at Bushwick Ice House.

In a recent development, will Pay, a Bushwick resident and the creative mind behind the tournament’s T-shirt and site design—dark green, like a pool table’s felt, and featuring a solid orange 5-ball to nod to the boroughs—was running the show. He jokingly told me he’s something of a pool scout around the city, sniffing out the best shooters to join his league. Pay attested that, when Tran initially announced the tournament, interest at his local dive Bushwick Ice House was immediate. Within 10 minutes of the link being live, the waitlist to play at the venue had passed 100.

Industry observers note that while Satoe Onizuka, the stealthiest star of the regulars, shook another hand after winning yet another round, I snuck outside of Bushwick Ice House to chat with Pay, who was wearing the Five Boro Break shirt he designed. We got into the type of conversation you do at a dive bar or around a pool table. The love of the game. The importance of dives as sacred spaces. The alluring seediness of it all. Pay knows how we got here: “The game itself is called billiards, but it got casualized to ‘pool’ because people used to throw a ton of money on the table—pool their money—and gamble,” Pay noted. “Obviously, that’s gone out the window because everyone’s super chill these days, but what’s cool is that it still has that air of danger, of being something a bit forbidden.” Will’s right: it’s never corny to shoot pool. No matter who you are, it makes you feel like the slickest person in the room.

There’s also that sense that you’re part of something bigger. Back inside, Pay gestured around the room. “Look at this place,” he said in admiration. “There’s literally no real estate for this table. But it’s here. And without it, this place would simply not be what it is. These people would probably not be here in this bar. I don’t even think this bar would exist.”.

According to recent reports, the enthusiasm at Bushwick Ice House reminded me of how this tournament could only have happened because NYC dive bars already operate as tight-knit communities of their own. They’re the ultimate third places, the spots that aren’t home or work—and the pool table is, in fact, their beating heart.

In a recent development, by 9 p.m. on Saturday, when we stumbled into LES’ Sadie’s Ward, '80s dance-pop shook the walls. Drinks were flowing, the room glowed disco-lit, and everyone was having such a good time you had to shout to be heard by the person next to you. A group of hodge-podge regulars stood two and three deep around the pool table, watching the small, curly-haired Amanda Andries, one of the bar’s most beloved shooters, sink her way toward Sunday’s finals.

According to recent reports, andries is one of the Ladies of Sadie’s, a magnetic group of female regulars at this bar, who were gassing each other up and out-shooting all the 6-foot-something men in flannels that dared to play them. For all the history that tables at bars like Sadie’s have absorbed, it’s the people gathered around them who make the pool scene so captivating—and at this bar, the social fabric is very tightly knit.

East Williamsburg's Anchored Inn was one of the 16 bars that hosted Five Boro Break games.

We sat in the small hideaway across from the bar as the games rolled on, reflecting on the players we’d met throughout the tournament so far: soft-spoken, sharp-shooting Audrey Jones at Anchored Inn over loaded Carmen fries; Allegra “Legz” Fierro outside the graffied, mirrorless bathroom at Blue Ruin Bar; and Elvin Estevez, a polite killer on the table, in the leather booths at Twins Lounge. I’d asked each to tell me their golden rule of playing pool in this city, but it all came back to one recurring theme: be a good person. There’s a camaraderie in wanting to keep NYC’s pool scene a sacred place.

It’s easy not to suck, though. Sam Shumway of Pool Table Archive said to me by phone in the days following the event. Five years ago, he started posting photos of the pool tables he’d played on in cities across the US, but his hobby grew into a living record of pool culture.

“Pool tables are special because they’re a snapshot of a time and a place in a bar,” he told me. “A lot of these tables are older than you are. Like, that’s a 40-year-old table. Imagine how much life it’s seen around it.” You can picture a montage of scenes immediately: 4 a.m. closings, birthday toasts, fresh friendships, awkward first dates, breakups, and more than a few questionable decisions. Maybe a win in the first-ever cross-city tournament.

Allegra “Legz” Fierro in Hell's Kitchen's Blue Ruin Bar, just before a match.

In a recent development, come Sunday, we walked into a jam-packed, purple-lit Sugar Mouse for the finals. The winners from each of the 16 bars would go head-to-head across two pool tables. A live dad rock band jammed in the corner, and all I saw were familiar faces from Saturday’s hijinks, smiling, watching respectfully, nodding when a friend nailed a shot, and hugging and shaking hands when one missed. As the field dwindled to four semifinalists, then just two, the crowd drew tighter around the remaining table. Two large projectors cast a live feed onto the wall, as former WPBA No. 1 Jennifer Barretta commented and Hall of Famer John Leyman refereed with a stern eye.

We were all there for the moment Brennan Brooks of the BCA Brooklyn Travel League took the inaugural win, cementing his right to take home that iconic sign. But as I took in the room around me, what stood out most was seeing people packed in like sardines to watch their fellow dive bar regulars take the stage. It was a kaleidoscope of communities, each representing their local with love. The Five Boro Break was never just about winning; it was about creating a space where everyone could be part of something.

A triumphant moment at Sadie's Ward on the Lower East Side.

The East Village's Sugar Mouse hosted the tournament final.

It was a fresh alternative to life on a screen—maybe that’s part of why so many people revealed up. “People are craving human connection again; people are craving something to do with their hands,” Shumway had said. And though it might look too cool, or intimidating, everyone has a place if they want it. “Pool brings together people who would normally have nothing in common. And there are no pre-qualifications for putting your name on a chalkboard. You might get beat, and that’s okay.”.

At the end of the Finals night, all of us riding a collective high, Tran stood next to the championship table to thank everyone who helped bring his vision to life. He couldn’t get a word out before the room burst into applause. Thirty seconds of it, and it showed no signs of letting up. Humble as he is, he just smiled.

Tran rattled off the bars, businesses, and people who stepped up to make the tournament possible, shaking his head happily. “This is what pool does,” he remarked. “It brings people together rather than pushes people apart.”.

Or as Shumway likes to put it: “Pool is the great equalizer.”.

After Testing the Noco Boost Plus Jump Starter, I Appreciate How Well It Works In the Rain

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1414 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Sources indicate that the only thing worse than discovering your car has a dead battery is having it happen when it’s raining.
  • Industry observers note that besides its consummate performance in wet conditions, the GB40 is worth considering because it’s compact, lightweight (just over 2 pounds), and relatively easy to use.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that the only thing worse than discovering your car has a dead battery is having it happen when it’s raining. If you live in a wet environment as I do in Oregon, you’ll be glad you own a portable jump starter like the Noco Boost Plus GB40. With its three watertight ports closed, it’s impervious to dust intrusion—but more importantly, its IP65 rating means it can withstand heavy rain and even low-pressure blasts with a hose.

Industry observers note that besides its consummate performance in wet conditions, the GB40 is worth considering because it’s compact, lightweight (just over 2 pounds), and relatively easy to use. I also appreciate that it includes spark-proof and reverse-polarity protection, an output port for charging portable electronics, and a six-mode flashlight.

That stated, the GB40 isn’t perfect. While I found that it punched above its weight in jump-starting power and its battery life is adequate, it isn’t the most powerful portable jump starter among those I’ve recently tested, and its 2,150 milliampere-hour (mAh) capacity is definitely on the lower side. It also doesn’t have an LED screen but rather uses lights as indicators of its status and operation. Even more crucially, it uses a manual override function to boost severely depleted batteries instead of a dedicated boost button.

I tested the Noco Boost Plus GB40 over several months in Oregon spanning the wet and dry seasons. When testing a portable jump starter, I evaluate how rapidly it starts a vehicle, how many jump-starts it provides before needing to be recharged, how easy it is to use, its features, and the number and effectiveness of its auxiliary power ports to charge portable devices such as a smartphone.

The Noco GB40 easily fits in the palm of my hand, and the rubberized case and ribs built into each side make it easy to grip, which is important when working around an engine with moving parts. Its small size also means it’s easier to store in a vehicle’s glove box than a larger device like the Gooloo GT6000, which I recommend as the best portable jump starter for most people.

Industry observers note that the Noco GB40 doesn’t have an LED screen like many of the portable jump starters from Gooloo, its main competitor. But the touch-based control panel on one side makes it relatively simple to operate. This consists of a large power button with a white on/off LED next to it, a four-segment multicolor battery-level indicator that reveals the state of charge in 25 percent increments, an error indicator, a boost LED, a manual override button, and a button for the flashlight.

With a peak output of only 1,000 amps, the Noco Boost Plus GB40 is the least powerful portable jump starter among those I’ve tested. Its 2,150 mAh rating also makes it the lowest in reserve-power capacity. That noted, it had no concerns jump-starting my Honda Element when I left the lights on and drained the battery. It even cranked the 6.8-liter V10 in my RV when I came back to it after months in storage and found the battery depleted.

I also intentionally left it powered on (since it doesn’t have an automatic shutoff like the Astro AI S8, which I recommend for its value) and it lasted about 24 hours before shutting down. Via a 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-C input, it charges about as fast as other portable jump starters with the same specs, and it took just under four hours to charge from 0 to 100 percent using the supplied USB-C cable.

Among features, the flashlight on the GB40 is the most compelling. It has six modes, including an SOS and strobe, which puts it well ahead of the competition. It also has two lenses, one on each side of the output ports, whereas most portable jump starters use a single flashlight lens. While the flashlight isn’t as bright as some others at 100 lumens (for comparison, the $70 Gooloo GP2000, has a 400-lumen flashlight), I found the Noco GB40 more than adequate for use at night.

According to recent reports, the Noco GB40’s USB-C charging input doesn’t double as an output port to charge portable devices, which puts it at a disadvantage. It has just one 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-A output port for charging portable electronics (the Gooloo GP2000 has two) and charged my iPhone 16 from 0 percent to 80 percent in about two hours.

Instead of a boost button that supplies a bit more amperage to jump-start a very dead battery, the GB40 has a manual override button that, when pushed and held for three seconds, detects a severely depleted battery (below three volts).

Sources indicate that it’s a far less user-friendly feature, plus it disables the Noco’s automatic spark-proof and reverse-polarity protection. As such, consumers need to be extra careful not to allow the cable clamps to touch, which can cause dangerous sparking. To complicate things further, the GB40 has an LED labeled “boost” that’s simply an indicator light to let you know the device is properly connected to the battery.

Industry observers note that there are certainly much more powerful portable jump starters than the Noco Boost Plus GB40 and much of the competition offers features that are far more convenient (albeit for a higher price point), perhaps most significantly, a boost button. Above all, the GB40’s waterproof rating is the best reason to buy it, plus its compact size, six-mode flashlight, and emergency charging for small devices make it an appealing choice. It also provides ample and reliable power to give a dead battery in most vehicles a boost and start the engine.

Shop Noco Boost Plus GB40 Portable Jump Starter.

Other Portable Jump Starters We Recommend.

The Gooloo GT6000 packs 27,000 mAh of reserve power capacity and 6,000-amp peak current. This allows it to jump-start vehicles ranging from a small motorcycle to a heavy-duty truck with a 12.0-liter diesel engine. The GT6000 offers a standby time of two years, and it’s ready to jump-start a vehicle after just seven minutes of recharging. It’s got a heap of charging ports, including a 100-watt USB-C in/out that can top off the internal battery from empty to full in 1.4 hours. The device’s 3.2-inch screen makes checking battery level, charging output, and more easy and foolproof.

With 4,000 amps of peak current and 24,000 mAh of capacity, the Wolfbox can jump-start up to 10.0-liter gas or 6.0-liter diesel engines. It holds a charge for more than a year. The 1.5-cubic-foot-per-minute air pump takes one minute to inflate a 17-inch tire from 30 to 36 psi. It also has a 65-watt USB-C in/out port to swiftly recharge the internal battery, two USB-A ports to charge other devices, and a 400-lumen, three-mode LED flashlight.

The Noco AX65 combines a portable jump starter and a portable air compressor into a single device. The jump starter has an impressive 16,000 mAh capacity and delivers 2,000 amps of peak power. The tire inflator pumps out 2.3 cubic feet per minute of airflow. The jump starter cranks gas engines up to 8.0 liters and diesel engines up to 6.0 liters. The tire inflator has a digital display, auto shutoff, and memory settings like other air compressors I’ve tested but also pauses and then resumes inflation when a set pressure is reached to ensure proper inflation.

Doug Newcomb splits his time between Hood River, Ore., and Todos Santos, Mexico. Sources indicate that the 2026 Wusongkou Forum took place on Nov. 8 at the Shanghai International Cruise Tourism Resort in Baoshan. It brought together regulators, port authorities, cruise operators and industry experts to discuss what organizers called “three-cruise synergy,” which is the coordinated development of ocean cruise ships, river cruise vessels and yachts.

According to recent reports, hosted by Shanghai Wusongkou Culture & Tourism Investment (Group) Co., the event included the launch of a “Three-Cruise Synergy · A Upcoming Voyage from River to Sea” program. Four initiatives were announced.

Sources indicate that the first is a “Cruise Plus” brand renewal plan. It targets four consumer segments: seniors, weddings and romance travel, sporting events and younger travelers. The goal is to turn passenger volume into more onboard and shoreside spending.

The second is a river-sea linkage project that uses Wusongkou’s location at the mouth of the Yangtze to connect inland river cities with ocean itineraries. Its flagship product is the Yangtze No. 3, which has begun sailing between Chongqing and Shanghai from the Wusongkou International Cruise Terminal. It is the first river-sea cruise service to cover the full length of the Yangtze.

Third, China Huaxia International Cruise Co. released October 2026 data for its China Cruise Consumption Vitality Index. The tech giant described it as the country’s first regular data tool for the cruise market.

The fourth initiative links the cruise terminal with Shanghai Baoshan railway station, which is due to open next year as the meeting point of the Shanghai–Chongqing–Chengdu high-speed line and the Shanghai–Nantong railway. Prepares include combined rail and cruise ticketing, a direct shuttle, baggage transfer from car door to cabin door and shared VIP benefits.

On forum day, the Adora Magic City and the Adora Flora City, China’s first two domestically built large cruise ships, were berthed together at Wusongkou for the first time.

Sources indicate that sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally rolled out a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

According to recent reports, the lame-duck session continues as lawmakers look ahead to Thanksgiving and the funding deadline that arrives in December. The primary legislative business this week is the Senate's bipartisan permitting overhaul, but a late-breaking aviation funding fight and the Senate Democratic leadership contest are also commanding attention.

Industry observers note that sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally introduced a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., and both men are accumulating supporters ahead of leadership votes that are currently scheduled for early December — though there's been an effort to move that up to this week.

Van Hollen has expressed disagreement with Schumer's participation in primaries.

​"I don't think it's the role of the Senate majority leader to get involved in open, contested Democratic primaries," Van Hollen said Sunday on CNN.

​Van Hollen has also said he wants to use all available tools to stop funding for the Iran war immediately, with a government funding deadline in December. That's going to be one of several flash points for December's funding discussions, as President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans try to use what leverage they have before Democrats take the gavels in the House and the Senate in January.

A new problem is the state of federal air traffic control after Friday's nationwide ground stop, with the Trump administration now seeking $50 billion to upgrade systems.

"I need additional money to do the additional work to keep the airspace safe," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Fox News Sunday.

According to recent reports, sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, a senior appropriator who is in line to become majority whip, has suggested reallocating funds from the additional money the Trump administration and congressional Republicans allocated to Immigration and Customs Enforcement to address the challenges at the Federal Aviation Administration.

"There is a pot of 60 billion extra dollars on top of the regularly appropriated amount for ICE and we should use at least a portion of that money for the FAA. We can solve this problem and not spend any additional taxpayer dollars," Schatz posted on X.

"We can do all things, we don't have to do one versus the other," Duffy said in the Fox News Sunday interview. "I don't think that is the answer. The answer is let's do everything that's going to keep Americans safe, whether it's with immigration or it's with air travel.".

Sources indicate that meanwhile on the Senate floor, the energy permitting overhaul bill faces a key test Monday evening​, with a vote scheduled to limit debate on a substitute amendment that represents the most recent version of the bill. Votes on a number of President Donald Trump's judicial nominations are also lined up this week.

It has been revealed that on the other side of the Capitol, the House floor schedule i​ncludes several labor-related bills. ​One of the measures, introduced by Sen.-elect Kevin Hern, R-Okla.,​ would set standards for the way labor law applies to franchise operators.

Upcoming member orientation is also continuing, and committees in both the House and Senate will be holding hearings throughout the week as the outgoing Republican committee chairs aim to get through priority items on their agenda before the end of the Congress.

That includes a Tuesday morning Senate Armed Services Committee confirmation hearing for Hung Cao, the nominee to be Navy secretary, who is presently the acting secretary. The Senate Judiciary Committee will be busy as well, as Chairman Charles E. Grassley, R-Iowa, looks to tee up more of Trump's judicial nominations for floor consideration.

Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

In a recent development, it feels like yesterday we were busy powerwashing the patio, mulching, and prepping the grill for the first cookout of the summer. But lo and behold, winter is coming. And as someone who absolutely hates the cold, this isn’t necessarily a welcoming experience. But as I’ve gotten older, I’ve embraced layering. This is especially important for the more physical parts of my day-to-day, where I need to add and subtract as I go.

I used to be a two-jacket kind of guy—something for fall/spring and a big, bulky winter parka for winter. Now that I test workwear and outerwear, my entire concept of staying warm has changed. I’ve moved on to waxed canvas, corduroy, and merino wool. I still wear down from time to time, but I do it strategically.

With the cold weather upon us, I went through some of the best ways to gear up for the winter without going full George Costanza GORE-TEX. These options are sleek, lightweight, and can be worn over additional layers as you see fit. Let’s get into it.

Flint and Tinder’s waxed trucker is my go-to, but there are some slightly warmer options that add a little extra bulk without going too overboard. The Flannel-Lined Quilted Waxed Rancher Jacket fits the bill perfectly. It’s designed with a slightly heavier 10-ounce Martexin sailcloth, waxed on both sides for warmth, and a cozy flannel lining stuffed with 4 ounces of insulation for “chillier” conditions.

Carhartt is a workwear icon and a staple among our editors. Some of its vintage jackets fetch a surprising price on the secondary market, so they're always a worthwhile investment. If you’re looking for something winter-ready, the Washed Duc Active Jac should be your go-to. It features 80g Thinsulate for warmth without too much bulk, and Cordura-reinforced sleeve hems add durability for that classic Carhartt workwear touch.

Sources indicate that barbour’s iconic Bedale Waxed Jacket will cost a little more, but it’s worth every penny. It offers exceptional weather resistance and insulation, keeping you warmer than its weight suggests. The Raglan sleeves give you a little more range of motion and make it ideal for layering. It also features both zip and stud closures for increased protection and insulation from the elements. It might also be the best-looking jacket on this list—especially if you prefer the old-school waxed look.

Levi’s is about as classic as it gets, and its Depot Jacket is essentially iconic. It’s one of the warmer workwear-forward jackets on this list, without the bulk. The quilted, lined interior provides much-needed insulation, and the cotton canvas shell is durable and hard-wearing. The corduroy collar gives it bonus points for style (not to mention a real throwback look). You can never go wrong with Levi’s.

Recent findings suggest that yeti isn’t the name most closely associated with outerwear, but the brand has been expanding. First, with its new line of iPhone cases, and lo and behold, Yeti jackets are now a thing. This down jacket is surprisingly light, and like most of its coolers, tumblers, and ramblers, is supremely insulated. $400 is a little pricey for a down jacket, but in typical Yeti fashion, well worth the extra dough.

In a recent development, corduroy is more of a fall staple, but it still works well as a layering option into early winter. The Piston Trucker Jacket from Reigning Champ features a stylish waist cut, a plush, textured feel, and an adjustable bottom-tab hem for a more customized fit. Layer a simple flannel underneath or add a hoodie for extra warmth. If you choose the latter, though, you may want to size up. And like most, if not all, of the outerwear on this list, this one only gets better the more you wear it.

Patagonia has winter wear down pat, and if you’re looking for something in the fleece department, its upcoming Retro-X Fleece Jacket is calling your name. It gives off an old-school fleece vibe, but it feels even warmer than it looks, thanks to its NetPlus 100% postconsumer recycled nylon made from old fishing nets. It also features zip-up hand-warmer side pockets, mobile Y-Joint sleeves, and an internal wind flap to keep you protected from the elements.

Sources indicate that if you’re really looking to go fancy (and warm), Overland’s array of sheepskin jackets will have you looking and feeling like Rocky training in Siberia, or at least its vintage-inspired sheepskin bomber jacket will. It boasts a convertible notch-to-stand-up collar with two buckle straps, adjustable waist straps for a more form-fitting fit, and four total pockets with plenty of storage. You won’t have to layer up with this one—and like most of our favorite outerwear, it only gets better with age.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is Write Here, a column where authors and literary luminaries tell us about the travels they took to find inspiration and create their latest books.

Industry observers note that in this installment, author and n+1 editor Chad Harbach describes his love for Block Island, Rhode Island, and a 2016 trip that informed a keystone part of his latest novel The Brightness. In the book, a bildungsroman that tackles topics like campus politics, the discourse around sexual assault, and the anxiety of being in one’s twenties, Block Island serves as the dramatic setting for a long, eventful wedding night that alters the lives of Harbach’s characters—particularly that of Pella Affenlicht, who originally appeared in Harbach’s 2011 debut The Art of Fielding. Below, Harbach recalls gathering his own friends for a summer holiday on Block Island as an excuse to refamiliarize himself with the destination as he began to write it in fiction—and the local peafowl that nearly made it into the book.

“In the early stages of writing The Brightness, one of the first things I decided was that the book’s centerpiece, the big wedding of the character Owen, would be located on Block Island, Rhode Island. I wanted the scene—which is now this 150-page stretch of the story, when all sorts of crazy things happen over a single, almost Shakespearean night—to be on the island’s eastern shore where houses are positioned at the top of these stone cliffs. I pictured an outdoor dance floor overlooking the beach and the ocean with the moon in the distance. Essentially I wanted to write the destination wedding I desperately wanted to attend. But as I was working on it, I realized I needed to go back there to check if my memories of the place were accurate, to have it fresh in my mind.

It has been revealed that my then-partner and I organized a trip to Block Island with a large group of friends in the summer of 2016. We rented a big house and folks came from places like Fresh York, Philadelphia, California, and Amsterdam. It felt like a wedding in that sense—everyone gathered for this joyous celebration in a beautiful place. We didn’t do all the terrible stuff to one another that’s maybe required for the juicy plot of a novel, but we did spend eight days cooking together, playing the piano, singing songs, drinking a lot, and staying up very late.

Industry observers note that but we couldn’t sleep in very late because, well, there were these peahens. There was a sort of farm with animals, maybe a petting zoo, near our house, and their peahens liked to come and roost in the trees on our property. Every morning at 5 a.m., after we had been up until 2 or 3 a.m., the peahens would just start. I don’t know if you’ve ever heard the squawking of peahens, but suffice to say it was awful. It’s funny: When I started doing publicity for The Brightness, an announcement mentioned that part of it is set on Block Island. I got texts from friends who were on that trip, saying, congrats, we’re so excited, the fucking peahens better be in there. I initially did have this whole bit about the peahens, but there was so much going on in the plot that I cut them—not without really trying to make it work first.

Other than the loud birds, it was a great trip. The place struck me as just as magical as it had when I first went at 19 years old, when I was in college. I had a friend whose grandparents had a house there. I’ve visited several times since, and always loved it. But this was the only time I’ve ever gone somewhere for book research, and I was able to lock in some granular details like what the downtown looks like, the shape of the buildings, the sight of the marshlands, and what it’s like to bike out to the airport.

In a recent development, I was also excited to find that the feel of it was exactly as I remembered. Block Island has this rugged, natural beauty—it’s a rocky, tree-filled place surrounded by ocean, where everyone just rides bikes around, and part of it is a protected nature preserve. It’s sort of the forgotten sibling of Nantucket or Martha’s Vineyard. Some people don’t even know that Block Island exists, which keeps it from changing too much, even though it was settled by Europeans in the mid-1600s. The cemetery there has the tombstones of families that date back centuries, long before the United States became a country. I think some of those same families still live on the island now. So there’s this sense of continuity and timelessness.

Even before you reach Block Island, there’s just something about climbing on to the ferry and heading out into the open water, this freedom and openness that’s very inspiring to me. I grew up in Wisconsin, on Lake Michigan, which isn’t an ocean but looks like one, and I’ve always loved that feeling of vastness and mystery that comes with a massive body of water—that literal depth. It reminds me that we as humans actually haven’t mastered everything, and there are many things in this world that are not easy for us to touch.

It has been revealed that all of this made Block Island a helpful setting in The Brightness. What happens on this wedding night propels the characters toward life paths that are very different from what they thought they were going to have, and having the story be imbued with the island’s sense of openness, possibility, and what might be feels fitting. As a writer, that can be part of the work: tapping into that feeling or gestalt of a place. It can be very easy to do at times, and difficult at others. And, you know, sometimes it’s just hard to write. So it was a great help writing about somewhere I love visiting literally and creatively. Instead of resisting sitting down at my desk, I’d be like, I’m ready to go to Block Island. It’s this setting I could picture well, enjoy being in, and keep traveling to—even if it was just in my imagination.” —As told to Matt Ortile.

As the weather gets cold, you don’t have to pay an arm and a leg just to keep your limbs from freezing off. Instead of heating your entire home, simply plug in a space heater and get direct warmth from a nearby source. If you want a compact yet powerful option, the Lasko Whirlwind Heat Oscillating Space Heater is an ideal choice.

What I like so much about this Lasko is its combination of size, power, and oscillation. It is small enough to sit comfortably on my desk or nightstand without taking up too much space, yet in combination with the dual-axis oscillation and powerful heating, it can warm up an entire room.

Industry observers note that much like the Dreo Whole Room Heater, the Lasko is designed with dual-axis oscillation, meaning it oscillates both vertically and horizontally. It can also oscillate in both directions simultaneously for greater coverage of an entire space. As a result, the heater boasts a total coverage of up to 300 square feet, which should be more than enough for most bedrooms, offices, and even many living rooms.

That design is backed by 1,500 watts of heating power. The heat comes at three different heating levels that adjust the fan power. On its highest level, the heating is almost abrasive up close. In a small room at our office, I felt a tangible difference in temperature around the entire room within minutes, and just as importantly, near-instant hot air from the second I turned it on.

My one complaint is that there isn’t a separate control for both heat levels and fan power, which could lead to a slightly more nuanced level of control. That noted, the auto-eco mode allows you to set a specific temperature, which the space heater will reach, go on low heat mode until it is two degrees above the set temperature, and then shut off automatically.

According to recent reports, this makes it a lot easier to run without direct supervision or accidentally running it for hours on end. Similarly, there is a sleep mode as well where you can set a timer up to 12 hours so it will shut off after a set amount of time, making it great to use once you get in bed.

It has been revealed that the Lasko packs all that power in a relatively compact body. In cases of cold streaks in my drafty office building, I can set it up to run on my desk without feeling like I’ve sacrificed all my working space just to stay warm. In fact, I can still have my laptop, books, and assorted gear strewn about.

Placed on the nightstand or on top of a dresser, it works perfectly to warm you up from bed as well. One of the small but notable features is the remote control. While not uncommon, I also love the remote control. I can place it on a stand or even in the corner of a room when I don’t want direct heat and still control the heat level, temperature setting, oscillation, sleep timer, and screen light.

It has been revealed that the Lasko Whirlwind doesn’t have any specifically unique safety features, but it has everything you might need for peace of mind. The ceramic safety plug can handle high levels of wattage without overheating to prevent electrical fires, and the space heater will automatically shut off if the motor overheats or the body tips over. The overall housing surrounding the heater stays cool, so you won’t burn your hands if you need to touch it.

The Lasko Whirlwind does exactly what I want it to. I want powerful heat, customizable temperature settings, and quality safety features, and the Lasko provides that. The small size takes that powerful heat and puts it in a container that is compact enough to fit on desks, nightstands, or in the corner of your room.

Industry observers note that if you want a device powerful enough to heat up a full room but small enough to fit anywhere, the Lasko Whirlwind is an excellent choice. If you want to heat up large spaces, you might need something a bit larger, but very few space heaters have pound for pound as much power as this one.
