Now hiring: Staff to power Democrats’ probes

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1230 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., arrives at the Rayburn Building for a House Judiciary Committee hearing in February.
  • Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the upcoming year, making the most of their coming majority.
  • That means staffing up major committees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., arrives at the Rayburn Building for a House Judiciary Committee hearing in February. He will be a key player in leading oversight efforts next year — and so will Democratic staff. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the upcoming year, making the most of their coming majority.

That means staffing up major committees. And for the dozens of attorneys and other aides preparing to take on a belligerent Trump administration that has cast Democratic oversight as potentially criminal, the job will come with extra scrutiny.

Arya Hariharan, former chief oversight counsel to Sen. Richard J. Durbin on the Senate Judiciary Committee and now a partner at Holland & Knight, said the pressure will be on from day one.

“Are you prepared to not sleep very much and know that every single thing you do is going to be scrutinized, every footnote, every comma?” Hariharan said.

Still, the way Hariharan sees it, serving on the Hill is worth it. “I hope they all fall in love with it because it’s a lovely place to work,” she indicates of staffers headed there for the first time.

The work done by attorneys and other staff in oversight probes can swiftly become part of constitutional law. When Trump adviser Peter Navarro defied a subpoena from Democrats investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, it touched off debates about executive privilege and contempt of Congress. Probes of Hunter Biden led to similar court fights.

Some questions have gone all the way up to the Supreme Court, like in Trump v. Mazars, when the House fought to access Trump’s business records during his first administration in furtherance of toughening up government ethics laws.

In a recent development, there’s every indication that pressure will continue in the new Congress. James Melendres, a partner at Snell & Wilmer, said Democrats are poised for aggressive oversight efforts, even if they know it could be tough to make headway against litigation resistant administration officials.

“Democrats are going to have less than two years to show results. I think they are going to move really fast,” Melendres stated.

Democrats will likely soon start to send out preservation letters to private companies, institutions and others they intend to probe in the new year, if they haven’t already, Melendres said.

Sources indicate that “There may be significant pushback from the administration, from agencies and individual government officials who receive requests. I think third-party, nongovernment agencies and individuals are going to be high on the list for these committees,” he stated.

In addition to the hiring that happens over the next few weeks, House Democrats will have major decisions to make about chamber and committee rules for the upcoming Congress, including who will hold subpoena authority. And off-Hill observers will be watching closely.

“For companies, for individuals and their counsel, mapping all of that is going to be a major part of the job between now and early January,” Melendres remarked.

Lawmakers need to nail down funding levels for congressional committees and staff — the amount of money involved can make a big difference in how big investigations get. Major committees, and major investigations, take a large amount of staff and expertise to get going.

For instance, the special House panel that investigated the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol spent about $14 million in less than 18 months, including for dozens of staffers.

Standing committees, such as Oversight and Judiciary, take a good chunk of change, too. In 2025 the House spent $12.9 million on the House Oversight and Government Reform panel, and $13.1 million on the House Judiciary Committee.

Those expenditures mean dozens of staff working long hours to review documents, send letters, send subpoenas and conduct interviews. Judiciary ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who is expected to serve as chair next year, remarked he wouldn’t get into specifics yet about how many resources the upcoming Congress may devote to oversight efforts.

“But we are talking about the most corrupt administration in the history of the United States, and this is an overwhelming and daunting task that faces us,” Raskin said.

The Trump administration itself has already signaled it intends to push back forcefully on congressional oversight efforts.

Earlier this month, President Donald Trump described Democrats’ vows to investigate his administration as “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”.

Days later, the White House counsel sent a letter saying that subpoena threats from House Oversight ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., and others “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”.

U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz for the Southern District of Texas followed up with letters of his own to Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn.; Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.; and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., urging them to preserve documents tied to their promised oversight.

“The American people are entitled to freely associate without their elected officials terrorizing them with aggressive, harassing government action,” Reitz’s letter to Warren remarked.

Members of the incoming majority have signaled they intend to defend themselves and their probes, and Blumenthal mentioned he won’t be deterred by the letter.

Industry observers note that “There’s no way that I’m going to be intimidated or bullied. It would be laughable and ludicrous, but it is a clear abuse and misuse of prosecutorial powers and weaponization by the Department of Justice,” stated Blumenthal, who serves as the top Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

As for Raskin, he called the White House counsel letter and other missives “absurd on its face.”.

In a recent development, “I’m sure they would love to get into a whole series of letters and counter-letters and litigation. They’re trying to distract everybody from the fact that they just lost the worst landslide electoral repudiation in at least a half century in America, and so they’re going to pick a fight,” Raskin told reporters.

Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely incoming speaker, told reporters last week that he intended oversight efforts in his chamber to be led by Raskin and Garcia.

According to recent reports, “We haven’t ruled anything in. We haven’t ruled anything out. We’re going to follow the facts. We’re going to apply the law. We’re going to be guided by the Constitution, and we’re going to let the chips fall where they may,” Jeffries said.

Democrats have already publicly listed a handful of job postings for oversight staff and counsel, ranging from the Science to Armed Services to Judiciary panels, set to start early next year.

Beyond those hires, House Democrats will have to make one major pick they haven’t yet unveiled — the House counsel. The position, first created in the 1970s, is hired by the majority and advocates for the chamber in court. That attorney, along with a group of bipartisan House leaders controlled by the majority, will steer the chamber’s legal strategy.

In prior Democratic Congresses, that office has been active in court; Doug Letter frequently argued on behalf of the Democratic House majority seeking to enforce subpoenas on behalf of congressional committees. The position is held by Matthew Berry in the current Republican-controlled House.

“I mean, I think a lot of people are interested in that job,” Raskin mentioned.

Review: Air France Hop! Embraer 170 Business Class (BSL-CDG)

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (684 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • My trip to Latest York on Air France began with a short domestic flight on the Embraer 170 in business class from Basel to Paris, a short and pleasant journey.
  • Years ago after my La Premiere flight from Los Angeles to Paris, I continued on to Basel on an Embraer 190 in what Air France marketed as business class.
  • But Air France has come a long way and I feel like even on a short domestic business class flight it really has really raised the bar in terms of service.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

My trip to Latest York on Air France began with a short domestic flight on the Embraer 170 in business class from Basel to Paris, a short and pleasant journey.

Years ago after my La Premiere flight from Los Angeles to Paris, I continued on to Basel on an Embraer 190 in what Air France marketed as business class. But the service onboard was no different than economy class: there was no blocked middle seat, meal, or beverages served in glass..it was just regular economy class service.

But Air France has come a long way and I feel like even on a short domestic business class flight it really has really raised the bar in terms of service.

I booked my ticket from Basel to Upcoming York JFK via Paris for 60,000 Flying Blue miles and $453 in business class, booking just 36 hours prior to departure (so yes, Air France does release last-minute award space).

Basel Airport straddles Switzerland and France. I entered on the French side and checked in for my flight.

On the check-in level you can walk back and forth freely between the French and Swiss side, but on the lower level and upper level there’s a physical barrier. For example, I went out to the terrace on the upper level and there’s a fence separating the two nations.

After visiting the Skyview Lounge, now operated by Aspire, I headed to the gate for boarding at 1:45 pm, which began right on schedule.

Stepping onboard, I found my seat in 2F.

It has been revealed that the aircraft has 76 seats in a 2-2 configuration. Each seat has 31 inches of pitch and is 18 inches wide. Seats recline three inches. There are individual air vents, but no power of any kind: neither USB or a universal power socket.

Business class can be adjusted according to demand, the “genius” of having the same seat. On today’s flight there were three rows of business class, but only three passengers: we each had our own row. Air France now blocks adjacent seats in business class, so that is a substantial advantage versus economy class.

The only other business class distinctive was that each seat had a pillow and water bottle:.

At only 250 miles, there wasn’t  much time for a meal service.

It has been revealed that air France nevertheless offers business class passengers a small meal box on its shorthaul network, part of a catering concept introduced in 2024 and developed with Servair Corporate Chef François Adamski, a Bocuse d’Or winner and Meilleur Ouvrier de France. For flights departing after 10:00 am, Air France serves what it calls a “signature” sandwich along with a French sweet or dessert, with the selection changing regularly. It is served in a sturdy cardboard box.

In a recent development, on my flight, the meal consisted of two finger sandwiches with smoked salmon and a creamy herb filling on brown bread, along with a small pecan tart and a chocolate…a very nice treat. The airline also serves wine and Champagne in proper glassware, though I just had sparkling water on this flight.

> Read More: Air France Served This Surprisingly Elegant Business Class Meal On A 250-Mile Flight.

Flight attendants onboard were very polite and efficient: meals and drinks were offered immediately and refills offered after they had completed service in economy class and again before landing, all on a very short flight.

This flight has no internet and no in-flight-entertainment, but Starlink is coming to these jets.

However, it was a beautiful day tempearture wise and I enjoyed looking out the window, especially as we flew over Paris (thought it was a bit hazy) as we neared CDG.

Recent findings suggest that business class passengers have a dedicated lavatory in the font of the cabin. It was small but clean.

We landed on time in Paris where I ran into a fairly complicated connection to Terminal 2E Hall M…but it was a short but lovely flight.

    #54099. Finnair Celebrates Men With An All-Male Crew While Some Airlines Still Won’t Hire Male Flight Attendants

    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Liveandletsfly ↗ Open Full Page

    Finnair Celebrates Men With An All-Male Crew While Some Airlines Still Won’t Hire Male Flight Attendants

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (897 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, finnair marked International Men’s Day with an all-male crew on a flight from Helsinki to London, drawing attention to how few men work as flight attendants at the airline.
    • Recent findings suggest that on November 19, 2026, Finnair operated flight AY1331 from Helsinki (HEL) to London Heathrow (LHR) with an all-male crew aboard an Airbus A350-900.
    • As noted by Ben from One Mile At A Time, Finnair says only about 10% of its cabin crew are male and would like that proportion to grow.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, finnair marked International Men’s Day with an all-male crew on a flight from Helsinki to London, drawing attention to how few men work as flight attendants at the airline. Encouraging women to become pilots and encouraging men to become flight attendants strike me as entirely consistent goals.

    Recent findings suggest that on November 19, 2026, Finnair operated flight AY1331 from Helsinki (HEL) to London Heathrow (LHR) with an all-male crew aboard an Airbus A350-900. The crew included two pilots and eight flight attendants. The gate agents were also men.

    As noted by Ben from One Mile At A Time, Finnair says only about 10% of its cabin crew are male and would like that proportion to grow.

    Recent findings suggest that I have flown Finnair many times and cannot recall ever having a male flight attendant. That is very different from my experience on virtually any other European carrier I regularly fly. My sample size is hardly enormous, but the statistic helps explain why this initiative caught my attention.

    Ben also addresses an interesting paradox at certain airlines, singling out IndiGo.

    The Indian carrier has good reason to celebrate its female pilots. In March, IndiGo announced that it had more than 1,000 women pilots, representing 17.5% of its pilot workforce. Yet its published entry-level cabin attendant eligibility criteria specify:.

    “Female Indian nationals, with Indian passport, between 18 to 27 years of age.”.

    That is an explicit restriction in the recruitment criteria, rather than simply a workforce in which women happen to predominate.

    It has been revealed that the nationality requirement is a separate question from the gender restriction. But the latter creates an odd contrast: women are encouraged to pursue a career historically associated with men in the cockpit, while men are excluded from this advertised path into the cabin.

    I agree with Ben that a boy who grows up wanting to become a flight attendant should be able to pursue that ambition, just as a girl who wants to become a pilot should. No, that does not mean every airline needs a precisely equal number of male and female employees in every role. Different people will make different career choices. But there is a considerable difference between who chooses to apply and who is allowed to apply.

    Flight attendants are primarily present for passenger safety, yet that does not make their hospitality role unimportant…I do not object to airlines making a polished cabin crew part of their brand.

    For example, I have no inherent problem with the glamour associated with the “Singapore Girl.” An airline can take pride in elegant uniforms and gracious service while ensuring its crew are trained and respected as safety professionals.

    But none of that establishes that hospitality is exclusively a female vocation. Singapore Airlines employs male cabin crew too.

    Industry observers note that I have been an usher at my church for 20 years, and I love that volunteer work. There is something deeply gratifying about welcoming people and helping them feel comfortable, including those who may be visiting for the first time.

    Recent findings suggest that I am not equating passing out service leaflets or collecting offerings with managing an aircraft evacuation! But there is an element of hospitality common to both roles, and I enjoy it. Men can—and should—be hospitable too. There is nothing inherently feminine about taking good care of another person.

    Sources indicate that if you have seen On the Basis of Sex, you may remember the case involving Charles Moritz, a never-married man who was denied a tax deduction for expenses incurred caring for his elderly mother. Ruth Bader Ginsburg and her husband, Martin, represented him. The law allowed the deduction for women and certain categories of men, but excluded a man in his circumstances.

    In Moritz v. Commissioner, the Tenth Circuit ruled in his favor in 1972.

    I cannot oversimplify by suggesting American sex-discrimination protections began with male plaintiffs. Ginsburg also helped secure the 1971 victory in Reed v. Reed, involving discrimination against a woman. But representing men disadvantaged by sex-based rules was an important part of her strategy. It helped demonstrate that assumptions about the proper roles of men and women could harm both.

    Industry observers note that ginsburg later discussed that litigation strategy, including the challenge of persuading judges and legislators who often viewed different treatment as protective of women. I find the principle relevant here. A rule premised on women being caregivers can disadvantage a man caring for his mother. A rule treating hospitality as women’s work can exclude a man perfectly capable of providing excellent service and can reasonably run afoul of public policy.

    Removing those restrictions benefits people who do not fit the stereotype, whichever sex they happen to be.

    An all-male Finnair flight is a small gesture, but one with a sensible purpose when men account for only about 10% of its cabin crew.

    Industry observers note that I welcome efforts to show people that an aviation career is open to them, whether that means a woman becoming a captain or a man becoming a flight attendant. I enjoy the elegance and hospitality that airlines can bring to flying. I simply see no reason qualified men should be excluded from providing it.

    According to recent reports, california Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, here at a 2020 news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center, is the chair of BOLD PAC. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Latino voters moved sharply away from Republicans this year, and a record number of Latino Democratic candidates were elected.

    It has been revealed that but California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez has a warning for her fellow Democrats.

    “Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” said Sánchez, who leads the campaign arm of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus.

    Failure to address rising costs and push back against President Donald Trump’s immigration agenda could once again scramble the political calculus and spark another realignment in two years, said House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar of California.

    “While Latinos shifted towards Democrats and … gave us this mandate as a party, Democrats must continue to earn their trust, not just every two years, but every single day,’’ he said.

    According to recent reports, leaders of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus joined newly elected Latino members on Tuesday for a news conference to celebrate the recent wins and the role the group played in securing the House majority for Democrats. The caucus will boast 55 members in the next Congress, its largest roster ever, according to Sánchez.

    BOLD PAC, the caucus’ campaign arm, invested heavily in Latino candidates this year, including in primaries.

    Recent findings suggest that california Rep. Salud Carbajal noted that BOLD PAC raised more than $18.5 million this cycle, which helped candidates leverage outside money.

    Working-class majority-Latino districts in South Texas, Arizona and California were among the areas that provided Democrats with their biggest wins. Democrats capitalized on voter dissatisfaction over rising costs, the very glitch that helped Trump and the GOP make significant gains among Hispanic voters just two years earlier.

    But the wins weren’t limited to districts with sizable Latino populations.

    Rep.-elect Denise Powell, who flipped a swing seat in Nebraska, credited BOLD PAC for playing a key role in her win.

    Industry observers note that “Yes, there are Latinos in Omaha, and those Latinos actually helped decide this race,’’ she remarked. “BOLD believed in me as a candidate, but they also believed in our community.”.

    Rep.-elect Bobby Pulido, who came to politics after a successful career as a Latin Grammy-winning Tejano singer, flipped a redrawn South Texas border district that Trump would have carried by 18 points in 2024.

    “A lot of people feel like they don't belong to either party. But there's one thing about Latinos is we belong to each other,’’ Pulido mentioned. “It's very hard to be a Latino right now in this country. … I expect to see us united, more united than ever, because it's a tough time right now.”.

    It has been revealed that several of the winning candidates deployed novel strategies to reach voters. Pulido famously began performing at quinceañeras after his Republican opponent dismissed him as a performer.

    According to recent reports, colorado Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, who flipped a battleground district north of Denver, attended World Cup and Broncos watch parties. “If people don't hear our message, then it doesn't matter,’’ he remarked.

    Recent findings suggest that the candidates “met those voters where they were,’’ Sánchez noted. “They went into those communities and interacted in a very real and meaningful way. That's something I think that strategists or consultants don't always get. It's not just about pumping out lots of television commercials.”.

    Amid those successes for Latino Democrats, Florida, home to one of the largest Latino electorates in the country, was a different story. Republicans held all three majority-Latino districts in the Sunshine State, though former news anchor Eliott Rodriguez, the son of Cuban immigrants, came within half a percentage point of unseating GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar in a district that backed Trump by 15 points in 2024.

    According to recent reports, BOLD PAC did have a victory to celebrate in Florida, with Rep. Darren Soto, the deputy chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, narrowly prevailing in a district that Republicans redrew as one that no longer had a Latino majority.

    “The redistricting wars ended up failing because of the investment by BOLD PAC,’’ Soto said.

    TAP Air Portugal will launch a fresh route to Washington, D.C., next year.

    In a recent development, starting March 30, 2027, the carrier will connect Porto and Washington Dulles. Flights will operate three times weekly.

    Currently, TAP serves Dulles from its hub at Humberto Delgado Airport in Lisbon. Its only U.S.-bound routes from Porto are to Boston and Newark, New Jersey.

    TAP officials said the upcoming connection will strengthen the airline’s presence in northern Portugal while expanding access to a vital foreign market.

    TAP serves Porto via Francisco Sá Carneiro Airport.

    The carrier serves nine destinations in the U.S., the others being New York-JFK, Chicago O’Hare, Orlando, Florida, Miami, Los Angeles, and San Francisco.

    #54095. Where Was 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' Filmed? Behind the Scenes in Spain and Germany

    Where Was 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' Filmed? Behind the Scenes in Spain and Germany

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (923 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television shows, and more.
    • We’re heading back to Panem for the sixth time this autumn, as the latest Hunger Games prequel hits screens.
    • Joseph Zada as Haymitch Abernathy and Whitney Peak as Lenore Dove Baird.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television shows, and more. This time, we take a look at The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.

    We’re heading back to Panem for the sixth time this autumn, as the latest Hunger Games prequel hits screens. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is set 24 years before the action of the first film and tells the origin story of Katniss Everdeen’s grumpy tutor, Haymitch Abernathy, as he enters the Games himself.

    Joseph Zada as Haymitch Abernathy and Whitney Peak as Lenore Dove Baird.

    Based on the books by Suzanne Collins, the dystopian series is set in a futuristic America in which each district must send a teenage tribute to fight to the death in an annual competition—the idea being that, by doing so, the public will be too afraid to rebel against President Snow.

    This edition of the games is known as the Quarter Quell, with double the number of tributes being sent into the arena, meaning the stakes are so much higher. Interest in the film is high, not least because Haymitch is so beloved in the original series, portrayed by Woody Harrelson. Newcomer Joseph Zada takes the lead role in the latest film, while Hollywood heavyweights Ralph Fiennes, Glenn Close, Elle Fanning, and Kieran Culkin also star.

    In a recent development, one of the most important sets in the film is the arena where the games take place, and for this, director Francis Lawrence opted not for CGI and a green screen, but instead a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve in northern Spain. Below, we look into the locations used in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.

    Ben Wang as Wyatt Callow, Percy Daggs IV as Ampert Latier, Joseph Zada as Haymitch Abernathy, and Mckenna Grace as Maysilee Donner in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.

    Within the book and film series, the settings for the Hunger Games are always known to be virtually spectacular. For this film, filmmakers settled on the vast and untouched landscape of Somiedo Natural Park in the Asturias region of northern Spain, which boasts mountain ranges, glacial valleys, beautiful meadows, dense forests, and tranquil lakes. The remote region is also home to the last brown bear population in Europe.

    When the tributes are launched into the arena, they are presented with a vast Cornucopia, a pile of weapons, food, and other supplies that might be useful to them in the competition. These scenes were filmed at Somiedo Natural Park, with the Asturian mountains and a glacial lake in the background.

    It has been revealed that “Somiedo is a spectacular place,” said Pedro Aráez, supervising location manager. “The valleys, forests, and mountains have a very wild, untouched feeling, which was exactly what the filmmakers were looking for. It’s remote, dramatic, and visually unique. When you arrive there, you immediately understand why it was chosen.”.

    Recent findings suggest that located close to Somiedo, the Teverga beech forest, Hayedo de Montegrande, was used for some of the dense woodland scenes, in which contestants battle it out and hide in the woods. Other scenes filmed here utilized a series of glacial lakes, the Saliencia Lakes and the Lago de la Cueva.

    Iris Apatow as Proserpina Trinket and Elle Fanning as Effie Trinket in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.

    In a recent development, before the tributes are launched into the arena, they are first held in special little pods underground which are arranged in a circle around the Cornucopia. The perfect location for this? A velodrome, of course, which is steeply circular so cyclists can race around it. The film crew utilized Berlin’s Velodrom for this very purpose, with its cold, clinical silver decor perfect for matching the hi-tech aesthetic associated with the Capitol.

    Ralph Fiennes as President Snow.

    Prior to entering the Games, tributes must introduce themselves on the public stage, during a televised grand chariot parade in the Capitol. Another Berlin location with links to the sporting world was used for this purpose: the Olympiastadion. For fans of the earlier films, this is the moment when Jennifer Lawrence’s character Katniss becomes “the girl on fire” with her incredible flaming dress.

    According to recent reports, the futuristic architecture of Edificio Calatrava in Oviedo, Spain—with its striking, claw-like structure—stands in for a building in the Capitol, where President Snow and his government live. The complex was designed by Spanish architect Santiago Calatrava, whose work is known for resembling living organisms. Meanwhile, the 14th-century Ehreshoven Castle, just outside of Cologne, was also used as a filming location, with local press reporting that its lush interiors might have been used to stand in for somewhere inside the Capitol.

    Sources indicate that A former smelting factory complex in western Germany, Landschaftspark Duisburg-Nord provides the backdrop for one of the most atmospheric settings in the films, Haymitch’s home of District 12. The vast complex is able to stand in for multiple places within the district, a former mining town that has fallen on seriously bad times. Rather than being a desolate area stumbled upon by the filmmakers, Landschaftspark is popular for its nightly light installation by British artist Jonathan Park. There are also regular al fresco events here, from film screenings to the annual art-meets-sport Ruhr Games and Traumzeit Festival. Another location in Germany, Lindlar Quarry, was used for District 12, with wooden huts built here to resemble the outskirts of the village.

    A version of this story originally appeared in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

    United Airlines CEO Says FAA Meltdown Was “Nobody’s Fault” And Wants Airlines To Help Fix The System

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1534 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that united Airlines CEO Scott Kirby thanked employees for helping passengers through the nationwide FAA disruption, singling out a crew that helped a mother with three tired children through the airport.
    • In a video message to United employees reviewed by Live And Let’s Fly, Kirby praised the airline’s recovery from the FAA ground stop and described conversations with administration officials and congressional leaders from both parties.
    • Industry observers note that he argued that fixing air traffic control requires more than money and asked for private-sector involvement in the process.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that united Airlines CEO Scott Kirby thanked employees for helping passengers through the nationwide FAA disruption, singling out a crew that helped a mother with three tired children through the airport. But his message also included a striking assessment of the crisis: it was “nobody’s fault,” and the private sector needs a greater role in fixing the system. I appreciate his focus on solutions, though that does not eliminate the need for accountability.

    In a video message to United employees reviewed by Live And Let’s Fly, Kirby praised the airline’s recovery from the FAA ground stop and described conversations with administration officials and congressional leaders from both parties.

    Industry observers note that he argued that fixing air traffic control requires more than money and asked for private-sector involvement in the process. But he began with the people who took care of passengers during the disruption, including the crew pictured above.

    Here is the full transcript of his remarks:.

    In a recent development, hello everyone, I wanted to come to you today before the holidays and say thank you for the amazing job that you did, taking care of each other and our customers during the FAA shut down over the past weekend. You really did do an amazing job. If I look at the numbers, our airline recovered better than any of our large competitors. If I look at the NPS scores, remarkable how positive they were because all of you were really committed to taking care of customers.

    It has been revealed that while I can look at the numbers, the anecdotes meant even more to me: the customers that I heard from, all the special things that our people, that all of you, did for customers really helped build the brand and really made all of us shine in a moment of difficulty. My favorite, perhaps, was that picture of the crew helping a mother with three young children get through the airport when they were tired and they were sleepy, and it hit two of the things that are really important to me: build an airline that is great for customers, and I think of that is make it easy for parents with young children to travel, but also an airline where our people committed to doing the right thing and taking care of customers.

    So thank you for all that you did working hard over the weekend and while you were working hard taking care of customers, I was busy on the phone talking to people in the administration, the leadership on both sides of the aisle in both the House and the Senate to really try to get this fixed.

    It has been revealed that so I’m not going to play the blame game because this has been building for decades. And the truth is this is nobody’s fault, but it is everybody’s responsibility to fix it. And it’s not just about money. It’s going to be about having a real process and having a real engagement to fix it. My request, frankly, is to let us be inside the tent. Let the private sector, we know how to do some of this stuff. We care about it more than anyone, for you and for our customers. And so I am committed, and I got great commitments from people on both sides of the aisle. Everyone wants to fix this but we need to stop talking about it and finally get it over the finish line.

    In a recent development, so thank you for all that you did to work really hard taking care of customers. Thank you for the best recovery of anyone in the industry. Thank you in advance for all you’re gonna do to take care of customers over the busy holiday travel that’s about to come up on us, so thank you. I’ll see you in the friendly skies.

    The photo Kirby referenced is my favorite part of this message too.

    Industry observers note that according to his account, the crew was helping a mother traveling with three young children. You can see crew members carrying children while others pull luggage through the terminal. Here’s the original Instagram post:.

    A post shared by Tammy Stull (@thetammystull).

    As a father who has traveled extensively with young children, I recognize how valuable an extra pair of hands can be!

    After a long delay, even the walk out of the airport can feel daunting (remember this?). A child falls asleep, another needs attention, and the bags (all of them) must carried. Someone stepping in to help can change how you remember the entire day.

    Kirby talks about building the United brand through those encounters. That is certainly true and I really like that he recognized this particular act of kindness in a message to the broader workforce. Employees should hear that helping a tired family is a core mission of the job and that employees are already stepping up in a beautiful way.

    According to recent reports, his claims about United having the best recovery and positive Net Promoter Scores are his assessment. That could be a classic Kirby exaggeration, but having flown last weekend myself, everyone seemed to be in a good mood despite a delayed departure.

    According to recent reports, I agree that America’s air traffic control problems have developed over decades. I also agree that another round of partisan finger-pointing will not modernize the system and in some ways is just not constructive.

    It has been revealed that but I cannot agree with the blanket assertion that this is nobody’s fault. There are two different challenges here: the longstanding condition of the infrastructure and the decisions surrounding the work that preceded this particular disruption.

    As I discussed yesterday, latest reporting raises questions about contractor supervision and changes to the FAA’s maintenance approval process. Those questions still require answers.

    Sources indicate that I take Kirby’s point to be that everyone should stop using the crisis to attack political opponents and start working together. That is a worthwhile appeal and one that I share. But identifying responsibility is part of preventing another failure.

    Industry observers note that if an oversight process was inadequate, it needs to change. If a contractor failed to follow required procedures, that needs to be addressed, no matter how often its work went smoothly in the past. If the agency lacked sufficient staff or technical expertise, the remedy should reflect that. We cannot reliably fix a problem while declaring in advance that nobody bears responsibility for it…but I’ll stop beating a dead horse.

    Kirby’s request for private-sector involvement is bold, but far too generalized to give us insight into the seriousness of that wish. Airlines have a direct interest in a functioning air traffic control system. Disruptions strand their aircraft and crews, cost them money, and leave their employees dealing with understandably frustrated passengers. Their operational experience should inform the modernization effort.

    But Kirby did not describe a specific governance proposal in this message. Asking to be involved does not, by itself, amount to a detailed blueprint for privatization or airline control of air traffic services. I would want to see what he proposes before endorsing or rejecting it…and wonder what it is that United or other carriers can bring to the table that would actually help the FAA.

    There is also an obvious complication: a private contractor was already involved in the work at the center of this disruption. Private-sector participation alone does not guarantee competent execution any more than government involvement guarantees failure.

    In a recent development, kirby’s observation that this is not just about money is very true. Fresh equipment requires funding. So do the people needed to install, maintain, and supervise it. But an appropriation cannot substitute for a sound implementation and oversight process.

    It has been revealed that I also appreciate he is holding conversations with leaders from both parties. That is the work airline executives should be doing when a problem this consequential affects their customers and employees…he has to be friends with everyone in the impending era of divided government.

    I made a similar point yesterday: Congress needs to investigate what happened while working with the administration on practical improvements. We do not need to choose between accountability and cooperation…let’s just get it done.

    Kirby can use his access to help advance that work. I hope he does.

    Kirby’s message combines well-deserved recognition for employees with an appeal to stop arguing and fix air traffic control.

    The crew helping a mother with tired children deserves the praise. His call for a serious process, rather than simply another demand for money, is true, but I liken it to a political talking point and working together should begin with an honest accounting of what failed. A willingness to cooperate is valuable: so is a willingness to accept responsibility.

    Sources indicate that in the meantime, that photograph is a welcome reminder that employees can still take excellent care of people during a deeply frustrating travel day. Kudos to those employees for practically showing, “Good Leads The Way.“.

    #54092. Airline Captain Defends 20-Year-Old Female Copilot After Fatal Learjet Crash

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1494 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Liveandletsfly ↗ Open Full Page

    Airline Captain Defends 20-Year-Old Female Copilot After Fatal Learjet Crash

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1494 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 121pilot, our resident commercial airline pilot on Live And Let’s Fly, examines what we know about the crash of Learjet 60 N722BD and pushes back against the rush to blame its young first officer, Nathalia Filgueiras.
    • Sources indicate that the crash of N722BD, a Learjet 60 operating on a charter flight, has drawn enormous attention.
    • According to recent reports, as is typical of the aviation YouTube community, many of whom I respect, people have been rushing to get videos out about this accident.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    121pilot, our resident commercial airline pilot on Live And Let’s Fly, examines what we know about the crash of Learjet 60 N722BD and pushes back against the rush to blame its young first officer, Nathalia Filgueiras.

    Sources indicate that the crash of N722BD, a Learjet 60 operating on a charter flight, has drawn enormous attention. Much of that is understandable. We have extremely dramatic video of the aircraft descending almost vertically at a very high rate of speed, along with equally dramatic ATC audio recordings.

    According to recent reports, as is typical of the aviation YouTube community, many of whom I respect, people have been rushing to get videos out about this accident. What I really don’t care for, however, are the clickbait titles. Titles like “Could Any Pilot Have Saved This Learjet 60?” or “Lear 60 Florida Crash: It Happened Before” or “Expert Pilot Explains What Likely Caused SHOCKING Plane Crash in Florida” by Megyn Kelly.

    These kinds of titles make me angry because, regardless of the actual content of the videos, they are misleading. The simple fact is that we know very little about this accident at this point, and certainly not enough to be speculating about a probable cause.

    Industry observers note that the aircraft, a Learjet Model 60 with nine people aboard, reported moderate turbulence and icing at Flight Level 350 and requested a climb to Flight Level 370. Moments later, the aircraft departed controlled flight, eventually entering a descent at an extraordinarily high rate of speed.

    We know that the NTSB has recovered components of the horizontal stabilizer that separated from the aircraft, and widely circulated video appears to show the aircraft without this crucial component.

    What we DON’T know is whether the aircraft flew into a thunderstorm. The weather imagery I’ve seen to date comes from sources that have time lags built into them and don’t necessarily represent the real-time weather picture. We don’t know what caused the horizontal stabilizer to separate, or even when that happened. Did it separate during the dive, or was its failure what initiated the dive? That’s an important distinction, and right now it’s an unknown.

    It has been revealed that we know the Learjet 60’s wing is sensitive to ice accumulation and that the aircraft is susceptible to a phenomenon called Mach tuck. We don’t know whether either played any role in this accident, or even whether the aircraft’s critical surfaces had accumulated ice.

    We know the aircraft had been operating at higher altitudes, with a reported descent from Flight Level 410 to 350 before the final sequence of events. But without knowing the aircraft’s speed, configuration, weight, and other performance parameters, we cannot draw meaningful conclusions about its operating margins.

    We know the captain was 55 years old and very experienced. We know the first officer was 20 years old and relatively inexperienced, but fully qualified to act as a second in command.

    Sources indicate that we know the CVR, or cockpit voice recorder, has been recovered, but we don’t yet know whether its contents can be successfully recovered or what information it might provide. We also know the aircraft was not equipped with a flight data recorder, or FDR. That means information about the aircraft’s speed, heading, pitch, roll, system status, and other parameters may remain unknown or will have to be reconstructed using external data sources and whatever information can be gleaned from the CVR.

    But perhaps the most disturbing part of this entire event, aside from the tragic loss of life, has been the reaction of so many people who couldn’t explain the difference between a slat and a flap, yet have felt perfectly qualified to judge the performance of the first officer based on her age and gender.

    In the Megyn Kelly video, she questions whether someone who isn’t even old enough to drink should have been acting as a pilot.

    Sources indicate that I think the better question is why we allow 18-year-olds to join the military and go into combat, but apparently don’t think they’re old enough to have a beer. Why can a 20-year-old warrant officer fly a Black Hawk full of troops into the maelstrom of a hot landing zone, but we think he or she can’t be trusted with alcohol?

    Even more disgusting have been some of the reactions to the ATC recordings.

    It has been revealed that first, let me suggest that if you haven’t already listened to them, don’t. Second, and most importantly, as a 56-year-old male airline captain, I hear absolutely nothing in that recording, either in her voice or in her actions, that merits criticism.

    Sources indicate that I don’t think people who haven’t experienced it can appreciate just how incredibly violent and terrifying that initial descent must have been. In one recording, we go from a seemingly calm situation, with the crew requesting a climb, to a loss of control and a reported descent of approximately 8,000 feet per minute in about 10 seconds. Just 16 seconds later, the aircraft is in an overspeed condition, and the first officer reports a descent rate of 20,000 feet per minute. That’s an absolutely eye-watering number. It defies belief and would be utterly terrifying to any pilot. About 10 seconds later, she reports that they are going to crash into the ground. Not long after that, someone can be heard in the background reciting the Lord’s Prayer.

    I don’t know this for certain, of course, but my suspicion is that somewhere during this sequence the crew became aware that the horizontal stabilizer had separated and that they had lost the ability to recover the aircraft.

    If there is anything to be stated about her performance as a pilot, it’s that she was clearly doing her job right up to the end.

    It has been revealed that we teach Aviate, Navigate, Communicate. Aviate means flying the airplane. Navigate means determining where you need to go and how to get there. Communicate means keeping the appropriate people informed.

    According to recent reports, in this situation, the captain was presumably concentrating on flying the aircraft while the first officer was communicating with ATC. That is exactly what we expect from a two-person crew in an emergency, assuming those were their respective roles at the time.

    According to recent reports, what’s more, in the absence of an FDR, the information she provided to ATC may prove absolutely crucial to understanding what happened. We may eventually discover that her actions and communications were instrumental in allowing the NTSB to piece together this accident. That information could well save lives in the future.

    Industry observers note that I also find it interesting, and troubling, that contrary to the media’s usual fixation on the captain, as though he’s flying the airplane solo, the exact opposite has happened here. The first officer has become the focus of an extraordinary amount of attention, even though we have not established who was flying the aircraft.

    It’s been my absolute privilege to fly with a number of female pilots throughout my career, and not one of them has ever done anything less than a sterling job. Frankly, the airplane doesn’t care about your gender or the color of your skin. And when it comes to aviation, that’s exactly how it should be. We should care about qualifications and competence. That’s it.

    Recent findings suggest that if I step onto my jet tomorrow and find a young female first officer waiting for me, I’ll be just as happy to have her there as I would a young male. At this point in my career, flying with a young and relatively inexperienced first officer gives me the opportunity to act as a mentor and pass along some hard-won flying wisdom. That’s something I genuinely enjoy. Nathalia had earned her place in that cockpit. Not one iota of the solid evidence we have right now leads me to believe that this accident can or should be blamed on her.

    According to recent reports, it may well turn out that crew errors figure prominently in the probable cause. We simply don’t know yet. But if that turns out to be the case, it’s important to remember that the captain was the pilot in command. He was responsible for the operation of that aircraft, and the first officer was serving under his command. If poor decision-making put the aircraft into a situation from which there was no escape, the captain would bear the primary responsibility for those decisions.

    Industry observers note that but that’s a hypothetical. And right now, we don’t know that any such decisions were made.

    We owe the nine people who lost their lives, their families, and the people who will eventually investigate this accident something better than speculation, sensationalism, and a rush to judgment.

    #54090. American officially retires its most exclusive long-haul seat: Bittersweet or overdue?

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (796 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thepointsguy ↗ Open Full Page

    American officially retires its most exclusive long-haul seat: Bittersweet or overdue?

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (796 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thepointsguy

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This week, the carrier (officially) bid farewell to Flagship First international service.
    • We’ve been talking for years about American’s plans to retire its international-style first-class product.
    • The airline is replacing Flagship First with larger and more modern business-class cabins on its marquee planes — cabins that will feature its next-generation Flagship Suites.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It’s the end of an era at American Airlines.

    This week, the carrier (officially) bid farewell to Flagship First international service.

    We’ve been talking for years about American’s plans to retire its international-style first-class product.

    The airline is replacing Flagship First with larger and more modern business-class cabins on its marquee planes — cabins that will feature its next-generation Flagship Suites.

    For a lot of flyers, that’s likely to be a positive shift: It will mean a host of upgrades in business-class, including seats with sliding privacy doors and superior tech.

    But there’s at least a little nostalgia in bidding farewell to a cabin that, for many years, was billed as American’s most exclusive.

    Industry observers note that american was the last U.S. airline that claimed to offer a standalone, international first-class product.

    Across the global airline industry, many carriers sunset long-haul first-class years ago, choosing to instead offer more — and improved — business-class seats, which take up less space and are considered more profitable.

    For years, Delta Air Lines’ Delta One business-class suites have been its premier long-haul offering.

    United Airlines bid farewell to international first class in 2018 when it pivoted to Polaris business class.

    Sources indicate that that left American’s Flagship First as a relic, of sorts, in the U.S. airline industry — and even on its own planes.

    In recent years, you could only find the cabin on two fleet types American operated: its Boeing 777-300ER, which offered eight of the pods up front in their own dedicated cabin.

    Plus, AA still (for now) offers Flagship First on its three-cabin Airbus A321T, which has been a fixture on lucrative coast-to-coast routes like Latest York to Los Angeles and San Francisco.

    But soon, it will be a thing of the past on both planes.

    American is retrofitting its larger 777s, ditching first-class in favor of 70 all-latest Flagship Suites in business-class — along with the biggest premium economy cabin it’s ever offered.

    Related: This is now American Airlines' most premium plane: Here's what it's like on board.

    On domestic routes, the A321T will actually keep flying with Flagship First through March 28.

    But after that, AA will stop selling the Flagship First cabin on the A321T configuration, which is eventually going away as American flexes in its new A321XLR planes fully onto its top cross-country flights.

    In a lot of ways, American ditching Flagship First is a positive (and arguably overdue) transition for flyers.

    It’ll give passengers more lie-flat seats to pick from, whether they’re paying cash, using AAdvantage miles or using a systemwide upgrade.

    Also — while those Flagship First seats were really spacious and comfortable, many would say that American's new business-class product is a major upgrade from what it previously offered in that cabin.

    On some planes, that even includes extra-spacious Flagship Suites Preferred in the front and bulkhead rows of some planes, which offer a lot more space.

    Value check: Is it worth buying up to American Airlines' newly introduced business-class Flagship Suite Preferred?

    Beyond the aircraft, American also aims to still offer many of the same amenities for business-class that first-class passengers historically enjoyed.

    Industry observers note that for instance, its Flagship business-class tickets get access to its premium lounges. Passengers traveling in Flagship Business and Flagship Business Plus on qualifying international, transcontinental and Hawaii routes will also be able to have a meal in its exclusive restaurant-style dining rooms in Dallas, Los Angeles and Miami.

    The experience is available on a space-available basis.

    So, in some ways, you could argue the end of Flagship First is more symbolic than anything.

    But for some AA loyalists, it's still a little bittersweet.

    TPG’s Clint Henderson is our resident Flagship First enthusiast, having flown the cabin on dozens of occasions.

    "The service in first class wasn't particularly differentiated, but I still liked a few of the special touches," he remarked, pointing to the additional soup course and appetizer, along with a handful of elevated amenities.

    He especially appreciated the “La-Z-Boy-style” seats at the front of American’s 777s, which could lie flat or swivel and turn into an “office in the sky.”.

    “While these cabins are definitely showing their age,” Henderson added, “I’m sad to see it go.”.

    While Flagship First is technically going away as an official cabin on international service, the seats themselves won't disappear overnight.

    So far, American has only retrofitted one of its 20 Boeing 777-300ERs that feature the seats. That means a handful of jets with the old first-class seats will still be flying around well into 2027.

    Sources indicate that going forward, the former Flagship First seats on those planes will be marketed as business-class. They won’t come with the full first-class service, but you’ll still get the elevated seat.

    The Best Hotels Near Disneyland Paris With Cinderella Suites, 'Toy Story'–Themed Rooms, and Quaint Cottages

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that located just 40 minutes from Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport, Disneyland Paris is the ideal place to begin a Parisian vacation or say au revoir before returning home.
    • There's also never been a better time to visit.
    • According to recent reports, of course, you'll need somewhere to rest your head at night, and that's where the best hotels near Disneyland Paris come into play.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that located just 40 minutes from Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport, Disneyland Paris is the ideal place to begin a Parisian vacation or say au revoir before returning home. Disneyland Paris's two theme parks, Disneyland Park and Disney Adventure World, pair timeless charm with an ease you'll never find stateside. Here, you can sip Champagne in front of Sleeping Beauty's castle—or visit a dragon beneath it—while filling your days with delightful architecture, unprecedented thrills, and the wildest wilderness ride Disney's ever built (Major Thunder Mountain!).

    There's also never been a better time to visit. Walt Disney Studios Park's March 2026 transformation into the new Disney Adventure World brought a drone-filled nighttime show, Avengers coaster, and even a Frozen-themed land featuring a lifelike Olaf robot to its once-faltering second gate. Now, between Fantasyland classics and futuristic favorites, there's something new and thrilling for the entire family to experience.

    According to recent reports, of course, you'll need somewhere to rest your head at night, and that's where the best hotels near Disneyland Paris come into play. Staying at a Disney-branded property typically affords guests special amenities including ticket packages, exclusive character meet-and-greets, and Extra Magic Time, which provides bonus time in the parks prior to opening. These hotels are great options, but can also be pricey—luckily, there are also a few non-branded properties in the area that make for great alternatives. There's something here for everyone and every budget.

    Industry observers note that unsure of whether you want to add something so Américain to your Paris vacation? As a theme park journalist who has visited all Disney parks worldwide, trust me: It's worth the visit. Even with so many cultural monuments in Paris, nothing is more delightfully uncanny than witnessing the United States section of It's a Small World. So, whether you're looking for glamour or simply a good location, read on for the very best hotels near Disneyland Paris.

    Distance from Disneyland Paris: Three-minute walk.

    It has been revealed that as the crown jewel of France's Disney resort, this 487-room property is Disney's best hotel overseas—and, quite possibly, in the entire world. After undergoing an extensive three-year overhaul, the iconic pink palace reopened in 2024 with princess suites and luxurious amenities worthy of its five-star ranking. Great for couples or families, guests can anticipate the ultimate royal treatment thanks to rooms with romantic castle views just steps from the park. With kids treatments at the Spa by Clarins and two complimentary hours of childcare each day, parents can unwind at the Fleur de Lys bar, enjoy a prix fixe meal at chef Jean Imbert's on-site restaurant, or perhaps even sneak back into the parks themselves. (We won't tell.).

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Distance from Disneyland Paris: Eight-minute drive.

    Rustic-chic in the best of ways, Marriott's Village d'Île-de-France offers cozy abodes that sleep up to eight with full kitchens, washing machines, and plenty of space to stretch out, all a short shuttle ride from the theme parks. Designed to emulate the charms of a small Parisian village, these quaint studios and multi-bedroom town houses feel more like cottages than traditional vacation rentals. Surroundings like these may sound quotidien to someone like Princess Belle, but the resort is as sweet as the rooms are spacious, making it an ideal choice for a hotel near Disneyland Paris as well as extended trips to nearby towns.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Distance from Disneyland Paris: 10-minute walk, 10-minute drive.

    Considering it's the only hotel in the world dedicated to Marvel's famed comic book characters, it's no surprise the Infinity Stone–colored beverages and slick, silver rooms at Disney Hotel New York - The Art of Marvel are somewhat out of this world. Family-friendly amenities like superhero meet-and-greets and a design studio with character drawing experiences make it the ultimate getaway for any comic book–obsessed fan in your family. Yet, even with hundreds of unique pieces of artwork, it won't feel like you're living through an Infinity War. Delicately executed details, like Manhattan Restaurant's Asgard-inspired chandelier and Spider-Man swinging across the panel screens at Skyline Bar, provide simple city elegance with the lightest touch of Marvel magic.

    Distance from Disneyland Paris: 17-minute walk, 8-minute drive.

    If this hotel reminds you of Walt Disney World's Yacht & Beach Club resorts, you're not mistaken—this 1,098-room Disneyland Paris hotel was inspired by its Florida counterpart. The nautical theming is strong, and it's that seaside charm that keeps parkgoers returning to this waterfront escape. Just a 15-minute walk from the park gates, guests can meet maritime Mickey & Minnie Mouse (who don delightful cruisewear) or indulge in a seafood buffet at the aptly named Cape Cod restaurant. It's modeled after a familiar location back in the States, sure, but after spending the day with princesses, dragons, and superheroes, you may find yourself overjoyed to return to those country club comforts.

    Distance from Disneyland Paris: 13-minute walk, 8-minute drive.

    Craving a bit more theming on your Disneyland Paris trip? Look no further than this national park–inspired escape. It offers lodge-style living perfect for a wintertime trip. Cozy up to the Redwood Bar & Lounge hearth, or in one of the newly renovated rooms with nods to Bambi and Pocahontas, and take in the charms of what Disney does best. Multiple on-site buffets allow you to feast like you've been on the move all day because, well, you likely have.

    Note that this Disney-operated hotel is at the moment undergoing a phased refurbishment. For stays in late 2026 and early 2027, I recommend selecting a refurbished room in The Lodges. Starting in February 2027, construction will move to general hotel spaces, and certain facilities will be temporarily unavailable.

    Distance from Disneyland Paris: 30-minute walk, 10-minute drive.

    Rooms at the boutique Hôtel l’Elysée Val d’Europe are modern and minimal, offering the perfect escape from any theme park chaos. Though it's just a 30-minute walk or a short, free shuttle ride away from the gates, the real perk of being a bit removed is its proximity to the Val d’Europe shopping complex and the designer outlet mall La Vallée Village. With a bounty of discounted prices on luxury brands like Prada, Saint Laurent, and Gucci, you're sure to find a Parisian souvenir that'll rival the array of Mickey Mouse goods sold within the parks.

    Distance from Disneyland Paris: Nine-minute drive.

    Recent findings suggest that if the City of Lights appeals to you for its style and romance, consider this your ideal hotel. Design-forward rooms with concrete walls, sleek bathrooms, and an open, plant-walled lobby offer reliable value without sacrificing taste, making it a perfect choice for travelers seeking something a little less Disney. While families will benefit from select rooms offering full kitchens and stovetops, the upgraded amenities—which include a heated indoor pool, sauna, and hammam—offer a little something for everyone, just beyond the parks.

    Distance from Disneyland Paris: 16-minute walk, 10-minute drive.

    Step right up to this quirky hotel that feels like a Western film set and is jam-packed with Toy Story details. Small touches, like cowprint bedspreads and appearances by Woody and Jessie, make Disney Hotel Cheyenne a hidden gem that's nearly as themed as Disneyland Paris's own Frontierland. Given that it's significantly more affordable than the majority of its Disneyland-owned counterparts yet retains perks like Extra Magic Time, this property offers a best-of-both-worlds approach for those who want to live a full Disney-fied day from first rides to fireworks.

    Distance from Disneyland Paris: 10-minute drive.

    Multi-room cabins at this expansive, woodsy resort are the perfect way to experience a taste of the outdoors between trips on Massive Thunder Mountain. Sadly, there are no theme park shuttle services, so parks must be reached by car, rideshare, or taxi. But that's not to say it's worth skipping—here, nature abounds in both form and function. There's an on-site aviary, comfort food at the Crockett's Tavern buffet, and plenty of rustic charm, so the comforts of home are never too far away. Consider this Disneyland Paris hotel as close as you can get to camping at Disneyland's theme parks—if camping also included unfettered access to Mickey waffles.

    What area is the best to stay in when visiting Disneyland Paris?

    Recent findings suggest that any hotel near Disney Village, the entertainment and dining district at the entrance to Disneyland Paris's two theme parks, is going to be the most convenient choice. This not only offers more ease and access, but affords you the option to shop and dine after the parks close each night. Still, booking nearly any Disney-operated hotel will give you benefits like Extra Magic Time and exclusive character encounters, which help get you even more out of your Disneyland Paris vacation.

    Are there any hotels that are walking distance to Disneyland Paris?

    According to recent reports, yes—but you might want to bring your sneakers. Disneyland Hotel is located directly at the entrance to Disneyland Paris, while Disney Hotel New York - The Art of Marvel, Disney Newport Bay Club, and Disney Sequoia Lodge are all a 10- to 15-minute walk through Disney Village to reach both parks. Disney Hotel Cheyenne is a further trek, about 15 to 20 minutes away, but absolutely doable. Shuttle buses are available as well.

    What is the 3-2-1 rule at Disneyland Paris?

    In a recent development, the 3-2-1 rule is essentially shorthand for how to streamline your Disneyland Paris experience. Experts recommend selecting three rides, two entertainment offerings, and one dining option for an easy, straightforward approach to planning a day at any Disney theme park. It works as well at Walt Disney World and Disneyland as it does here at Disneyland Paris, but I recommend you still do a little research before you go. Be sure you don't skip Phantom Manor, which can only be found in Paris, secure your dining reservations early, and don't miss the nighttime reveals offered at both parks—they're among the best in the world.

    It is best to stay within the park at Disneyland Paris, or outside of it?

    It goes without saying that the closer you are to the castle, the “better” your hotel will be, but it shouldn't be a deal-breaker. Convenience is always a factor, but Disney-operated hotels at Disneyland Paris tend to be much pricier than their American counterparts, so staying a bus ride away might be necessary. Still, the perks are plenty across most of Disneyland's own hotels, including extra time in the parks, which is why I recommended so many of them.

    Industry observers note that A flight attendant signing with a young passenger is a lovely moment on its own. But seeing five-year-old Luca meet American Airlines CEO Robert Isom, who learned a few signs to greet him, made me smile even more. We spend plenty of time examining what airlines get wrong. Here is something American got right.

    It has been revealed that luca is five years old, Deaf, and loves airplanes. In a video shared by American Airlines, a flight attendant communicates with him in sign language near the aircraft door and. again onboard. Watching Luca respond is delightful.

    Sources indicate that there is something particularly sweet about seeing a child discover that someone outside his family can communicate with him in his own language. The flight attendant takes the time to engage with Luca directly, and his reaction is precious.

    The family later shared footage of a visit to American Airlines in Dallas, including a meeting with Isom.

    According to his mother, Isom took the time to learn how to spell his name and sign “nice to meet you” in American Sign Language. He also gave Luca American Airlines trading cards, which she said he was very excited about.

    Her explanation of why the meeting mattered was simple:.

    “I can’t tell you how much it means when someone takes that extra step to communicate with him.”.

    A post shared by CALLIE FOSTER (@thelacouple).

    According to recent reports, in another post about the visit, she described hundreds of American employees gathering to welcome Luca, with many having learned some sign language for him. She stated the family had not known what American had planned and was overwhelmed by the reception.

    The same goes for the employees who learned signs before welcoming him. It is easy to talk about the need to “care for people on life’s journey” (the current AA slogan). Here, they did something practical to make that happen.

    Sources indicate that as a father, I understand why his mother was so touched. When someone makes an effort for your child, you remember it. A brief interaction that an employee might regard as a small part of the workday can become something a family talks about long afterward.

    Sources indicate that and yes, American shared the encounter on social media. I am glad it did. There is room to recognize good hospitality even when an airline benefits from showing it.

    It has been revealed that between the flight attendant signing with Luca and the welcome he received at American’s campus, this family has some wonderful memories to take home. I appreciated watching Isom make the effort too. Learning a greeting is a modest undertaking, but his mother’s account explains how much it meant. Well done to everyone at American who helped make Luca feel so welcome. This was a refreshing bit of airline news to watch.

    #54086. American Airlines Offers “His” Free First Class Upgrade For $91, Then Tells Frequent Flyer To Delete His Complaint

    American Airlines Offers “His” Free First Class Upgrade For $91, Then Tells Frequent Flyer To Delete His Complaint

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1039 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that an American Airlines frequent flyer complained about a $91 first class upgrade offer and received a response asking him to delete his post.
    • This hit my algorithm on X (and apparently VFTW too), but an AAdvantage Executive Platinum member took to the platform to express frustration that American was offering paid first class upgrades for $91 while his complimentary upgrade had not cleared (this was on a short 551-mile flight from Dallas to El Paso).
    • American acknowledged his frustration, then added:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that an American Airlines frequent flyer complained about a $91 first class upgrade offer and received a response asking him to delete his post. That might sound like an airline trying to suppress criticism, but there is a much more sensible explanation: his screenshot exposed his reservation details. As for the inexpensive upgrade itself, I see a pragmatic opportunity rather than a scandal.

    This hit my algorithm on X (and apparently VFTW too), but an AAdvantage Executive Platinum member took to the platform to express frustration that American was offering paid first class upgrades for $91 while his complimentary upgrade had not cleared (this was on a short 551-mile flight from Dallas to El Paso).

    American acknowledged his frustration, then added:.

    “Please delete this from public view and join us in DM.”.

    The response attracted attention, but the screenshot included the passenger’s reservation confirmation number. That is a good reason to remove it and not a sign of AA trying to hide from its transactional upgrade policy!

    It has been revealed that we can understand why this feels frustrating. Your loyalty is genuinely appreciated, and we're sorry this experience left you feeling overlooked. Please delete this from public view and join us in DM.

    — americanair (@AmericanAir) November 18, 2026.

    It seems obvious to me that American was trying to protect the passenger here.

    A reservation confirmation number, often called a record locator or PNR, is something you should keep private. Combined with your last name, it can potentially allow someone to retrieve your booking. Depending on the airline and its security controls, that could expose information about your trip or allow someone to interfere with it. At least with AA you also need your birthdate in order to access the record online or on the AA app.

    Posting a screenshot to make a point about upgrades should not mean giving strangers an opportunity to tamper with your reservation…and some losers have far too much on their hand (which I’ve found out the hard way and why even when I “live blog” I never truly live blog).

    Industry observers note that american could have explained this much better. A simple request to remove the screenshot because it contained private booking information would have avoided the ambiguity. The passenger could then have reposted his complaint with those details obscured.

    Recent findings suggest that as to the underlying complaint, I understand why an Executive Platinum member would be frustrated. If you have directed substantial business to an airline and are waiting for an upgrade, watching the airline offer that seat for a relatively small payment can feel like your loyalty counts for very little.

    But I am not going to attack American for selling inexpensive upgrades. This is the business model now, and I use it to my advantage when I fly AA. If the economy fare is attractive and American subsequently offers a reasonably priced upgrade, I can evaluate the total cost and decide whether first class is worth it. Sometimes it is. Sometimes I am perfectly happy staying where I am, like on a recent flight where I ended up with an entire row to myself. Oddly, sometimes the cost of the upgrade is more than buying the ticket outright…I have no explanation for that.

    That is a much more straightforward transaction than spending more throughout the year in the hope that an airline will eventually reward me with a seat it would still prefer to sell.

    Recent findings suggest that fundamentally, a complimentary upgrade that has not cleared, even at the gate, is not a seat that already belongs to the elite member. We can debate all day long about how prominently or aggressively airlines market upgrades when frequent flyers are waiting when upgrades are dangled like a carrot on a stick, but passengers can respond to that change by reconsidering how much they are willing to spend pursuing status.

    I am a free agent, and it is liberating. More people should try it. Two years in, I’m more happy than ever (and flying in first class more than ever on domestic flights). I  choose a flight because the schedule works or because the price makes sense, without worrying that I am depriving my preferred airline of another qualifying flight or dollar toward next year’s status.

    According to recent reports, if American offers a good fare and an inexpensive first class upgrade, great. I can take advantage of it. I do not need to be an Executive Platinum member to recognize a good deal (as much as I miss the oneworld emerald lounge access when traveling internationally).

    Industry observers note that that does not mean status has become worthless. I still receive occasional complimentary upgrades as both an American Airlines Gold and United Airlines Gold member. I appreciate those upgrades very much, especially when I am not expecting them. But I do not build my travel intends around them. Hoping for a free upgrade seems futile in many cases even with top-tier status, particularly when the airline business model now centers on actively trying to sell the remaining seats.

    Industry observers note that for me, an occasional upgrade is a pleasant bonus on a flight I was otherwise willing to fly in economy class on. But upgrades are not a compelling reason to keep spending more with one airline when another offers a better flight….sorry, but the value proposition is gone.

    Sources indicate that american Airlines could have been clearer about why it wanted this passenger to delete his post. Still, the exposed reservation details provide a sensible explanation, and I would not characterize the request as an attempt to silence criticism.

    As for the $91 upgrade, I am pragmatically happy those offers exist. They give me another way to sit up front without organizing my travel around the pursuit of top-tier status. I still enjoy the occasional complimentary upgrade, but choosing flights on my own terms, and paying for a better seat when the price is right, has been far more satisfying than chasing an upgrade that may never clear. Try it, you’ll like it.
